items.sum: Report of the final track fixture of the season at Imber Court, a four-club match won by Belgrave against the Metropolitan Police, Herne Hill and Mitcham A.C.
items.s: Match v. Metropolitan Police Report of the final track fixture of the season at Imber Court, a four-club match won by Belgrave against the Metropolitan Police, Herne Hill and Mitcham A.C. Our final track fixture took place at Imber Court, the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police, and Herne Hill and Mitcham A.C. were also present. The sprint events were 1st and 2nd string races and Ivan Mayers scored a good double when winning the 100 in 10.4 and the 220 in 22.5 secs. Alan Law was second in the other 100 yds. race, while D. Gordon was third for us in the 2nd 220 yards Ian Badiali won the 440 yds. in the good time of 51.5 secs., and Jack Brown was second to Terry Higgins in the 880 in 1 min. 57 secs., with Alan Bishop in third place Ray Tooby ran an impressive race to win the 1 mile and his time of 4 min. 18.4 secs. was said to be a new ground record. We were pleased to see Vern Blowfield win the 2 miles run and his time of 9 min. 42.6 secs. was good, seeing that he had to slow down over the last 100 yards owing to Achilles’ tendon trouble. Our lads were also second to Herne Hill in the medley relay in which Badiali ran a good quarter to give us the lead, but over the 330 yds. stage Alan Bishop found that his two previous runs had taken the edge off his speed and he handed over in third place to Ivan Mayers. The latter went off as if he was jet-propelled and soon passed the Mitcham runner, but could not catch Higgins who was leading. Alan Law ran the final 110 yds. and he came in an easy second with Mitcham third and the Police last. We also did well in the field events and Jack Chappell was very pleased with the good response to his “ cards ” and is already looking forward to great things from his section next season. E. M. Bare won the high jump with 5ft. 10in., P. C. Luxon had a busy afternoon in winning the long jump with 21ft. 2in., being 2nd in the javelin throw and also second in the triple jump. Our Polish member, T. Gaworski, won the weight with 42ft. 1in., which must almost be the best ever by a Club member, and then was second in the discus throw. They also included a 120 yds. hurdles event and a Hammer Throw and while we could not field anyone in the former event, we had P. L. Porter in third place in the latter. So ended a good afternoon’s sport in which we had a very good muster of members present, and the final match points were: Belgrave H., 65; Met. Police, 50; Herne Hill H., 47; Mitcham A.C., 35. items.sum: Report of Belgrave performances at the City Charity floodlit meeting and the London v. Paris v. Brussels contest at the White City in September.
items.s: The Floodlit Meetings Report of Belgrave performances at the City Charity floodlit meeting and the London v. Paris v. Brussels contest at the White City in September. The first of these was held at the White City on 10th September and was the City Charity meeting, in which we had several members competing for their various business associations. In the sprints we had I. A. Mayers, our coloured sprinter, gaining 3rd place in the 100 yds. final, while in the 220 yds. he was 3rd in the fastest heat with only the first two going forward to the final. Ian Badiali won his 440 yds. heat in 51.9 secs., and was placed 5th in the final, which was in 49 seconds by Arthur Wint who was running for the Hospitals. Bob Taylor won his 880 yds. heat in 1 min. 59.7 secs., and was only narrowly beaten in the final in 1 min. 57 secs. Jack Brown ran his best mile of the season to beat Gordon Pirie in the fast time of 4 mins. 13.4 secs., which was a record for this meeting and also a personal best for Jack. Ray Tooby ran a fine race to win the 2 miles’ run in the excellent time of 9 mins. 12.2 secs., which was a new meeting record, and he beat D. H. Holden, K. L. Norris, R. H. Dunkley and P. J. Pirie to mention just a few of the large field in this race. We had C. R. Jones in the High Jump while Dennis Fleming threw for the Police in the Javelin Throw, and it was interesting to note that the Weight was won with 41ft. 11in., which puts our new member Gaworski in a favourable light. The second of these floodlit meetings was the London v. Paris v. Brussels contest also at the White City on the 17th September, and a large crowd saw a very interesting evening’s sport. In the 5 miles’ walk, which was billed as an attempt on the world’s record, Roland Hardy, of Sheffield United Harriers, was pulled out and the rest of the field never looked like getting near the record. Denis Merrett and Basil Walden were down as reserves for the 100 yards race, but as McDonald Bailey and Brian Shenton were present, their services were not required. Bob Taylor was also down as a reserve for the 880 yards, but here again the two first strings, Day and Hewson, turned out, so Bob was not called upon to run. As the winner’s time was 1 min. 56.6 secs., with the two London representatives doing 1-57.3 and 1-57.6, it will be seen that Bob would have been well with them. Jack Brown was the first London string in the 1 mile race, and he fully justified his selection by beating his opponents in 4 min. 18.4 secs., after appearing to be boxed-in coming down the finishing straight. In the medley relay race Alan Sexton ran the 110 yds. leg, but as Arthur Wint gave London a tremendous lead over the opening 440 yds., the rest of the team did not have to hurry themselves. John Bromley ran in the 3,000 metres steeplechase at the end of the meeting, but was well behind even though he managed to finish in front of one of the Brussels runners. The final points were: London, 130½; Paris, 81½; Brussels, 70. I. A. Mayers I. A. items.sum: Report of Belgrave finishing 5th in the Surrey Road Relay, a race they had won since its inception, with stage times and final placings.
items.s: Surrey Road Relay Race Report of Belgrave finishing 5th in the Surrey Road Relay, a race they had won since its inception, with stage times and final placings. Having won this race since its inception, it was a bit of a shock to find us only finishing in 5th place in this year’s race. This was due mainly to the fact that owing to John Bromley being unable to turn out, we had to call on a reserve in Don Maclean, and he ran sadly below his usual form. There were ten clubs competing, and at the end of the first of the six “ legs ” we were in 9th position and about a minute and a half behind the leaders. Arthur Bruce pulled us up three places on the 2nd stage and Chas. Walker brought us to 5th on the third leg, and we then ran Jack Braughton in an endeavour to overhaul the leaders. Jack ran a fine lap in 14.7 which was only 5 seconds outside the course record set up by C. J. Chataway, but could only improve one place, and as S.L.H. had Gordon Pirie on the next leg it was not surprising that Len Adams dropped back to 5th once again. Eddie Short ran our final lap of about 3 miles, and although he caught Butler, of Surrey A.C., he was eventually beaten on the final run-in by about a yard. Our runners’ times were: Maclean, 15.50; Bruce, 14.22; Walker, 14.50; Braughton, 14.07; Adams, 14.37; Short, 14.33. Final placings and times were: 1, Herne Hill H., 87.07; 2, South London H., 87.45; 3, Walton A.C., 88.00; 4, Surrey A.C., 88.19; 5, Belgrave H., 88.19. items.sum: Report and results of the London to Brighton walk on 13 September, with Belgrave's "A" team 4th and "B" team 11th behind Poly Harriers.
items.s: London to Brighton Walk—September 13th Report and results of the London to Brighton walk on 13 September, with Belgrave's "A" team 4th and "B" team 11th behind Poly Harriers. We mustered 16 entries, comprising two teams for this event and of the total only one was a non-starter, our new member, Norman Guuimant, who decided at the last moment that he was not quite fit enough and so spent the day as Percy Wright’s attendant. Most of our lads seemed to take it fairly easy at the start, and it was some time before any of them were anywhere near the front. Hugh McGreechan eventually pushed forward a bit but had rather a bad time about half way and began to drop back. Meanwhile Harry Shields, who was suffering from a boil on the foot, showed great pluck in keeping going and Fred Rolfe looked certain of a faster time than last year. Our fourth man, Jack Wakeley, was not far away, but making a check at half distance, it looked almost impossible for us to be placed, whilst there seemed no doubt that Poly would take team honours. Although our scoring four finished before Woodford Green or Highgate, we had to be content with 4th place. Poly. Harriers, with their four in the first seven, scoring 19 points, beat our record low score of 21 points in 1936. The usual useful work was carried out by the cyclist attendants and special thanks are due to three members of the Police Cycling Section (not Belgrave members) who came along to assist some of our walkers. In this race the runners go off in accordance with their time allowance and George Still was first away followed by Jimmy Flatt. Another old-timer in George Tyrer was present but only as an on-looker. When they came in sight of the finish our old friend Bert Mitchell was in the lead followed by young Dick Savage, with a new youngster in E. Cronk in third place. Eric Herbert was coming through very fast, but was just unable to gain a place, and we expect he felt the effects of his mountain-climbing effort in Wales. items.label: No. 116
items.sum: Report praising Syd. Spencer and Fred Herring for completing the Bath to London 100 miles walk inside 24 hours, and thanking the club helpers.
items.s: Bath to London 100 Miles Walk Report praising Syd. Spencer and Fred Herring for completing the Bath to London 100 miles walk inside 24 hours, and thanking the club helpers. In this tremendous feat of endurance we had three heroes actually walking and several smaller heroes who gave unselfishly, but with much personal inconvenience, their help to our walkers, and in fact to other walkers and officials throughout the race. We cannot speak too highly of the wonderful efforts of Syd. Spencer and Fred Herring. Syd., walking in his first 100 miles, was quite happy all through the race and gave his faithful helpers not too hard a time. Fred Herring’s performance was outstandingly courageous. Fred has failed to secure his Centurion’s Badge in five previous races and his tenacity in attempting continuously to obtain his 100 miles status is to be admired. This tenacity was outstanding during the second half of the race and we are delighted at his success. Gordon Doubleday, already a Centurion, was forced to retire owing to lack of sleep during the week through preparing the Belgrave accounts. Belgrave should feel satisfied with their share in this enterprising and successful promotion. Mention must be made of Joe and Percy Wilson, Harry Shields and Jack Goswell, who cycled all the way from Bath with our men, Jack Stirling-Wakely who walked about 65 miles with Fred Herring, Percy Wright and Bert Clayton who were willing helpers during the night in the wilds of Wiltshire, Frank Elson with his wife and daughter who arrived at the half-way mark at 3.30 a.m. and continued throughout the race giving encouragement and help. At Slough, Belgrave had a feeding station well manned by Syd. Roberts, Jack Rutland, George Checkley, Fred Rickards and Frank Thomson. Frank is particularly mentioned for his tremendous effort in regaling the walkers from first to last with Horlicks and sponging, and it was truly amazing to see such vitality from one of his age. Well done, Frank, the walkers did appreciate it. But after giving credit to all these, our real heroes were undoubtedly Syd. Spencer and Fred Herring, and they deserve most wholeheartedly our congratulations for their grand courage and success in walking this 100 miles inside the 24 hours. Syd. Spencer Syd. items.s: Club Five Miles Handicap—11th October, 1952 Report of the club 5 miles walking handicap on 11 October 1952, incorporating a match against the M.P.A.A., won on handicap by new member C. MacLennon. Fine weather gave us a good start to our Winter Road Season. This year our 5 miles handicap race also incorporated a match against the M.P.A.A., and 35 walkers started. Sid. James and George Oliver could be seen leading the field, with Paddy Woods and George Checkley following close behind. Down the hill positions closed up and there were little packs of walkers together. Back on the Common, Sid. took a slight lead on Paddy, but coming down Lauriston Road, Paddy came again, and they finished together in 37-42, with George Checkley 3rd. The handicap was won by our new member, C. MacLennon, who walked well to finish in 42-20, and with 7 minutes allowance he beat Percy Wilson by 5 secs., with W. Ferguson third. Another good job by Billy True who seems to have us all in line. Scoring 12 a side we lost to the M.P.A.A. by 108 points to 192 points. Sid. James Sid. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the third Southern Road Relay on 11 October, won by Belgrave in 3 hrs. 48 min. 34 secs. with several stage records, with Belgrave stage times and the first six clubs; it says both that Eddie Short beat the course record and that Norris of T.V.H. deprived him of it.
items.s: Southern Road Relay Stage-by-stage report of the third Southern Road Relay on 11 October, won by Belgrave in 3 hrs. 48 min. 34 secs. with several stage records, with Belgrave stage times and the first six clubs; it says both that Eddie Short beat the course record and that Norris of T.V.H. deprived him of it. The third of these races for Southern clubs only was held on October 11th and 20 clubs had been invited to take part. Notable absentees were South London H. and Aylesford Paper Mills, but Thames Valley, who had won in 1950, were competing this time. On the first stage from Mitcham to Purley we had Jack Brown, and he put up a truly magnificent performance to beat Alec Olney’s record time of 27.37 by five seconds. He gained for us a lead of 33 seconds with Walton in second place and Cambridge third. Chas. Walker went off next, and although he did 7th fastest time for this relay he lost 32 seconds, so that at the next change-over we were only a second in front of Essex Beagles with Walton in third place. On the third stage we ran John Bromley and he really had a poor run, in fact there were only two slower times than his and he not only lost the lead but dropped us to 6th place, and we were now 2 min. 14 secs. behind the leaders, Essex Beagles, with Walton A.C. second and Thames Valley third. Arthur Bruce on the 4th leg put in some fine running to not only beat the course record by 13 seconds, but he took us back to third place, a second behind Herne Hill, and he had gained 1 min. 13 secs. on the leaders. Ray Tooby also put in a record-breaking run on the 5th lap and he beat the old record by no less than 37 seconds and gained 35 seconds on the Essex Beagles’ runner, who also beat the old record, and we were now second with Herne Hill third. Bob Taylor, on the short 6th stage, gained 8 seconds on the leader, but we were still 18 seconds behind Essex Beagles, with Herne Hill still in third place. Jim Peters was the next runner for Essex Beagles on the long 7th relay, and seeing that he broke the course record, it was not surprising that he gained ground from Len Herbert. Len, however, was below his usual form and he actually lost 2 min. 12 secs., so that we were now 2½ minutes behind the Beagles with Herne Hill still hanging on to that third position. It now looked like a win for the Essex team, but Len Adams had other ideas and, running like a man possessed, he not only beat the course record by a second, but he gained 1 min. 28 secs. on the leaders and we still had a fighting chance. Eddie Short evidently thought so too for he also beat the course record by a second and not only gained 1 min. 2 secs. on his rival but caught him about 100 yards from the change-over and swept by him to give Bill Lucas a lead of 9 seconds. Bill has done this last lap into Brighton on previous occasions and he made no mistake in going right away from his rival and actually gained 45 seconds, so that our winning time of 3 hrs. 48 min. 34 secs. was only 5 seconds outside the record time put up in 1938 by Mitcham A.C. It is obvious that but from the bad time had by John Bromley, and if Len Herbert had been up to his last year’s form, that we would have “ smashed ” the course record and whether we have now missed our chance of doing so, remains to be seen. That conditions were ideal is shown by the fact that records were broken on all stages except the third, which some people think was never accomplished. It is liable for timekeepers to err! Club records for this race were broken by Jack Brown, Arthur Bruce, Ray Tooby, Len Adams and Eddie Short, and it was a pity that Norris, of T.V.H., beat Eddie’s time, thus depriving him of the course record, but the other four now go on the list of course record-holders. items.s: Highgate Open—25th October, 1952 Report and results of the Highgate open seven miles walk on 25 October 1952, in which a depleted Belgrave team did not share the honours for the first time for years. Nineteen of our lads faced the starter for the opening seven of the season. Unfortunately we were minus three of our scoring team of last year, and for the first time for years Belgrave did not share the honours of the Highgate seven. After the usual scrambled start our lads took the hill easy, and passed the top in 27, 28, 30 and 31st position with the others all fairly close. Down to the Bye-Pass positions had changed, the leaders were Barratt and Mash together followed by Coleman, with Sid James 7th, George Oliver 19th, Gerry Warr 20th and G. Checkley and P. Wright 34th and 35th, with all the others well up. Round about 3½ miles we lost Sid James and M. Guilmant who displeased the Judges and with Cambridge, Highgate and Woodford well up our team chances were negligible. At the Castle the leaders were the same with the lads in 16th, 25th, 29th, 32nd and 36th positions, and so down the East End Hill and on to the fields to the finish. Final Result being, Barratt 1st, Mash 2nd, Richards 3rd with Gerry Warr 18th, G. Oliver 23rd, P. Wright 25th and G. Checkley 34th. With depleted forces we say “ Well Done Lads ” and to Bernard Eglinton, P. Wilson and J. Haynes (a newcomer), we send our congratulations, they are improving every time out and walked really well, and we certainly have a basis for a good “ B ” Team. Keep it up lads, Good Luck. items.s: Club 5 Miles C.C. Handicap Report and full results of the club 5 miles cross-country handicap at Wimbledon on 25 October, with a match against Maidenhead A.C.; Jack Brown and Ray Tooby ran in together and J. E. Burr won on handicap. This was held at Wimbledon on October 25th and we had the Maidenhead A.C. as visitors to our quarters also the members of the Veterans A.C. who were also holding a handicap event in conjunction with our own race. There was a field of just over 70 runners who were despatched on their journey by our President, and as it had been decided not to go through the Brook, they did a lap and a half of the starting field before going out across the golf course. Ellis of Maidenhead showed the way in the early stages with Chas. Walker going up to him but before very long Jack Brown and Ray Tooby had taken command. This was the order in which they came back to the finishing field and Jack and Ray ran in together for first place with “ Ginger ” Newell showing a welcome return to form in gaining third place. Eddie Short came next followed by Ellis, and the next Maidenhead man was in 18th position so it will be seen that they found the opposition a bit too strong for them. The handicap was won by J. E. Burr, a fairly new member, with Doug. Briggs second and J. McDonald third, and the latter must have found it a change from the usual long-distance runs which he has been indulging in. items.sum: Editors' introduction to the Road Running Section notes, answering a complaint about missing road reports, with notice of the next Open 20 miles on 16 May 1953.
items.s: Road Running Section Editors' introduction to the Road Running Section notes, answering a complaint about missing road reports, with notice of the next Open 20 miles on 16 May 1953. In a recent News Letter published by the Road Running Section some comments were made about the absence of Road Running Reports in the “Belgravian.” We, your Editors, feel that this is not quite fair. We are very anxious to include reports of all sections, but unless we receive some notes or articles in brief we cannot invent them. We certainly have received on one or two occasions some literature which we claim we have included in the “Belgravian.” But now that the Road Running Section is recognised as a very live section of Belgrave we do assure you that the Editors do not now wait for reports, but worry the section's literary experts into submitting them when required. This fact, we know, will readily be admitted. We are glad, however, to report that the Road Runners have indeed been very active and there is no doubt also that they are a happy and exceedingly enthusiastic little band well led by Denis Brickwood and Arthur Whitehead. They have their own News Letter which gives their members all the gen, but we report here, necessarily briefly, all their activities for the benefit of other Belgravians and also for the purpose of Club Records and History. First of all, would all members please make a note of the date of the next Open 20 miles—Saturday, May 16th, 1953. Denis Brickwood Denis Brickwood leads the Road Running Section Arthur Whitehead Arthur Whitehead leads the Road Running Section Open 20 miles

items.sum: Report of the first Annual London to Brighton run sponsored by the Road Runners Club, won by Reynolds of Blackheath in record time, with Belgrave third team and Wally Wortley 10th.
items.s: London to Brighton Run Report of the first Annual London to Brighton run sponsored by the Road Runners Club, won by Reynolds of Blackheath in record time, with Belgrave third team and Wally Wortley 10th. Yet another chapter in the Club's long and successful connection with the Brighton road opened on the 27th of August when five of our road runners were among the fifty odd starters in the first Annual London to Brighton run sponsored by the newly formed Road Runners Club founded by our Vice-President Ernest Neville. With excellent weather and with such fine runners as the Blackheath trio Reynolds, Piper and Busby and Tom Richards, Paterson and Henning competing, it was generally anticipated that Ballington's record would be in danger, and Reynolds put up a magnificent performance in lowering it by 1 min. 20 secs. covering the 52¼ miles in 5 hrs. 52 m. 22 s., no less than 16 mins. ahead of Hefford of Woodford Green who was second with Henning third. In the team race Blackheath were again successful with Woodford Green second, Belgrave third and the Metropolitan Police fourth. From the start our new Member Wally Wortley ran extremely strongly, and in finishing so high up in such a distinguished field put up a really remarkable show. He will be a most valuable addition to our road running section when he has qualified to represent the Club. Our Marathon champion, Macdonald, despite a bad spell at about forty miles when he was nearly caught by George Chantler, finished very strongly, and George running his usual steady race also did very well indeed to finish inside seven hours. Arthur Whitehead after running with George to over 35 miles faded badly but managed to complete the course to make up our Team, which did very well to close in in such an exacting race at the first attempt. Arthur Penstone, suffering from an atrocious cold, did well to reach the 35 mile mark, but was soon afterwards forced to retire. Our runners wish to express their warmest thanks to fellow Members who suddenly showed up at odd points along the course with words of encouragement. In a long slog of this sort supporters can make all the difference between dropping out and carrying on. For Ron Linstead and Joe Stevens who acted as Attendants no praise can be too great. Without their help our runners could not have competed. Positions were as follows:— 10, Wortley 6 h. 28 m. 34 s.; 16, McDonald 6 h. 38 m. 20 s.; 17, Chantler 6 h. 50 m. 18 s.; 21, Whitehead 7 h. 14 m. 58 s. items.sum: Account of the Nijmegen Four Days' Marches of July 1952, where Jack Wakeley marched in the R.W.A. team and five Belgravians in the M.P.A.A. police team, with lessons learned.
items.s: NIJMEGEN MARCHES—1952 Account of the Nijmegen Four Days' Marches of July 1952, where Jack Wakeley marched in the R.W.A. team and five Belgravians in the M.P.A.A. police team, with lessons learned. Among the 10,000 participants in the Annual International Four Days' Marches held at Nijmegen, Holland, from July 22nd to 26th, were six Belgravians; one—Jack Wakeley—in the R.W.A. Team, which took part in the 55 Kilos event, and five in the M.P.A.A. Team marching in Police uniform with a small (1 kg.) pack in the 50 kilos section, which the writer had the pleasure of leading. Jack Wakeley, the present English 100 miles Champion, with previous experience of the Marches behind him, was naturally one of the stalwarts of the R.W.A. team, and as Billy Baker's tribute in the Race Walking Record shows, he did the job in true Belgravian fashion, helping the English team to maintain its usual 100 per cent. performance and win a team award. Hugh McGreechan, Frank Jarvis, Sid Spencer, Jock Ferguson and I, with 13 other members of the M.P.A.A. met with a few of the troubles which first timers in the Marches encounter, but came through with only one casualty and so secured the coveted Corps Medaille. Inexperience led me to put our tallest men in front on the first day, with almost disastrous results for the shorter men of whom Jock Ferguson came off worst; so severely were both his feet blistered that after the second day of what must have been crippled agony (he was never heard to complain) he had to be ordered, on the doctor's advice, not to walk on the third and fourth days. Sceptic blisters are not funny and, how he finished on the second day is a mystery and a tribute to his grit. Sid Spencer had few competitors for the title of fittest man of the whole team, whilst Hugh McGreechan, who found it all well within his capacity, was heard to complain only when the singing stopped. Frank Jarvis had one difficult patch on the first half of the fourth day, but was as usual full of chirpiness and was never in danger of failing to finish. I had one or two patches of heavy weather, but found it well within the range of anyone reasonably fit. It was certainly great fun and a truly wonderful experience. We found that the 11 hours allowed each day for the 31 miles was ample. Marching at about four miles an hour with two or three stops, totalling 1½ to 2 hours, left us with 60 to 90 minutes to spare. There is of course no question of racing and, in fact, fast marching is frowned upon. One team which got in very early on the first day were made to wait about for nearly an hour before being booked in! The Marches were as usual magnificently organised, and the Dutch clearly have immense pride in them. It is a fact that the Nijmegen Medal awarded to those who complete the marches is authorised to be worn in their own armed forces with an individual's gallantry and campaign medals. Among the lessons we learned were:— (a) First and foremost must be the care of the feet. Shoes or boots must be comfortable; big enough to allow for at least some swelling of the feet and really stout in the sole, if only for the occasional cross country stretches. All regular marches seem to make Rule 1 that of strapping the heel and the ball of the foot with narrow strips of plaster, slightly overlapping, with similar protection for the large and smaller toes. I tried this after the first day and thereafter had no trouble at all, which seemed to be the general experience. (b) The next care is to have plenty to eat. We found Dutch fare very good indeed, but of course different from English in some respects and liable to cause a few people in times of extreme tiredness to lose their appetite. Ten hours of open air exercise leave no doubt about the importance of this however, and quite obviously it is a Team Captain's No. 2 care to see that no one neglects his feeding. (c) No. 3 is the question of rest. My team gave no trouble at all and we all had an hour or two in bed as soon as we had finished, and most were down to it again by ten o'clock. Rising at 3.15 a.m. for a 4.30 start makes this a vital matter. (d) Marching in step proved best for us and to music better still; whether to a mouth organ or to our own, at first, unaccustomed and hesitant voices. Tipperary got a little too thoroughly plugged, but like “She'll be coming down the mountains” is quite international and both were sung by almost every foreign unit we came across. Also internationally popular was one beginning “Roll me over,” which I had not, I think, previously heard. Everyone in the M.P.A.A. team seems quite determined to go next year and enquiries about chartering a plane again have already been made; which one feels is recommendation enough. With care, i.e., spending little on beer or presents, the week's trip can be done for about £17 to £18, which is no more than a week at the seaside. Individuals may enter on their own, subject of course to the usual consent of the A.A.A. or join the team which the R.W.A. organises every year. Better still, if I may make a suggestion, would be a Belgrave team; we need only ten and it really is almost child's play to those who are reasonably fit—as of course most Belgravians are—people like Bert Footer for instance!!! But if he goes, I go with the M.P.A.A. again. items.sum: Frank Simmons' message to the club's juniors congratulating them on the season, urging winter training at Battersea Park and Belgrave Hall, and welcoming new members.
items.s: To All Juniors Frank Simmons' message to the club's juniors congratulating them on the season, urging winter training at Battersea Park and Belgrave Hall, and welcoming new members. First let me congratulate the Junior athletes of the Club on their performances throughout last season. It was a pleasure to me to see so many support our fixtures and indeed, I had a job to fit everyobdy in. But I like it that way, for it shows we have in the making good club members who will turn out on any and every occasion. Some of you may still be at school and if you have a school match on the same evening as the Club, then your first loyalty is to your school. Loyalty to me means, if you have a duty to perform, whether at home, at school or in the club, then do your utmost to carry it out. This brings me to a point which I wish to make clear—the making of promises. Many of you promised me that you would train during the winter, well what about it? I have not seen many who made this promise, or was it made just to stop me badgering you about training, for believe me, you will not and cannot improve on broken promises and no training. The weather may be bad, good or indifferent: wet, dry, warm or cold; but we are always at Battersea Park Track on Saturday afternoons from 1.30 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. and Sunday mornings from 10.30 a.m. to 1 p.m.—that is of course, those who are keeping the promises they made, and myself, with Franz Stampfl, who has never failed to turn out for his coaching sessions. I hope those who made this promise to me will have a great sense of guilt in not keeping it. Those who have come along so far can, I am sure, honestly say they have enjoyed themselves in the happy company of Belgravians assembled and on their behalf I extend a cordial welcome to all those who wish to come along and have a rattling good time at our coaching and training sessions. John Jones, Dave Ansell and C. R. Jones are three who have trained regularly and industriously so far and I am looking for great improvements in these and many others in field events. I cannot stress too much the importance of training and ask you to get down to it NOW. You cannot afford to waste any time. I am holding Wednesday evening indoor coaching at Belgrave Hall from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. and a programme has been worked out which will cover all angles of field events. You do not have to pay anything extra for this—it is all included in the very small annual subscription which you pay. Make it worth me giving up my time, often at cost to myself and the other coaches who are willing to assist you in your chosen events. To the Cross Country juniors and youths, on behalf of the track boys, I wish you every success this winter and hope you will exceed all your expectations. Make Mickey Pyer a happy man by winning the National Junior C.C. He is a grand fellow whose first consideration is YOU and such a great success by Belgrave Juniors will be much appreciated, especially by Mickey. To the Junior walkers—“Keep 'em down” and have a go. You have a great tradition behind you that should be enough to spur you on to great heights. To follow in the footsteps of Tommy Green, Harry Churcher and many others too numerous to mention. To those who are now entering the Senior ranks of the Club, carry on the grand work which you started as a Junior, and to those just joining the Club as Juniors, we give you a hearty welcome and want to make you happy in this happy band of Belgravians. Finally to all juniors in the Club, may your successes be great and your disappointments few. May we all go forward together along the road of high endeavour to make this our greatest year so far in the Club's history. Frank Simmons FRANK SIMMONS Franz Stampfl Franz Stampfl coach at Battersea Park Track sessions John Jones John Jones junior, training regularly Dave Ansell Dave Ansell junior, training regularly C. items.sum: Progress report on plans to rebuild Belgrave Hall, which may close for the summer of 1953 if a building licence is obtained.
items.s: Belgrave Hall Progress report on plans to rebuild Belgrave Hall, which may close for the summer of 1953 if a building licence is obtained. After many months of legal wrangling, with letters by the dozen, things have at last sorted themselves out, our dreams for rebuilding the Hall are now beginning to take shape, plans have been prepared, builders are estimating, with a general easing of the labour market, and a more plentiful supply of material, there is every possibility of our obtaining the necessary licence, if this is forthcoming, we plan to start building at once, this will mean, that the hall will be closed for the summer months, members normally using the hall, are asked to make alternative arrangements, while no definite date of completion can be given, members can rest assured that every effort will be made to have the hall ready for the beginning of the winter season 1953. T. F. Morrell T. F. MORRELL Hon. Sec. "House" Sub-Committee Belgrave Hall

items.sum: Club news column: births, Jack Chappell's elections, members' track and walking successes, National Service postings and G. Walsh's running in Singapore.
items.s: Here and There Club news column: births, Jack Chappell's elections, members' track and walking successes, National Service postings and G. Walsh's running in Singapore. Although a little belated, but none the less sincere, we send heartiest congratulations to Alf and Mrs. Harley on the birth of their twin daughters and we are glad to know they are all progressing favourably. Congratulations to Jack Chappell our Field Events Hon. Secretary on his election to the office of President of the South of the Thames Cross Country Association and Vice-President of E.C.C.U. and S.C.C.C.A. Among the successes by our members during the past track season were—Ray Tooby who won the Junior Inter-Banks 1 mile race in 4 min. 28.2 secs. Jack Brown 2nd in the Civil Service 1 mile with Bob Taylor 3rd in the 880 yards. J. D. Benstead was 3rd in the Southern Junior 220 yards, while Frank Wright was 3rd in the A.A.A. Junior 880 yards and also finished 3rd in the Junior half-mile at the British Games meeting in the fine time of 1 min. 57.4 secs. Jack Brown also ran 2nd to [illegible]oger Bannister in the A.A.A. v. Combined Services match in 4 min. 16.6 secs., and also finished 3rd in the 1 mile event at the Highland Games held in Edinburgh. Bert Jordan won the 7 miles road race handicap at the Oxted meeting on August Monday. Ian Badiali won the Shipping A.A. 440 yards championship in 52.1 seconds, and Len Rolls won the Veterans A.C. 880 yards championship. Ted Smith won the London Transport 7 miles Walk Championship at Wembley in record time. Harry Shields was third. Quite a number of our lads are now having to join up to do their National Service training and recent joinings include—Peter Casselton to the R.A., Charlie Henn to the R.E.M.E., Peter Courtney who managed to get placed in the half and mile at his Depot Sports. Brian Trower writes us from the Fighter Plotters School at Middle Wallop, while J. Hills is with the R.A.S.C. at Aldershot, and Don Maclean is now with the R.A. in North Wales and says he is hoping to get in some running while there. Vern Blowfield also writes to say that his family are now with him at Oxford, but that he hopes to come up for some training runs and says he is looking forward to having a good season and takes it as a good omen that the Southern is at Aylesford, as in 1948 at the same venue he was 3rd in the individual race, while we won the team championship. A feature of the finish of the Southern London to Brighton Road Relay was our large crowd of supporters holding a club banner, made by the President's wife for the occasion, and it is hoped to include a photo of this in the programme for next year's race. G. Walsh, a Corporal in the A.C.C. in Singapore is apparently making his presence felt out east. As there are no English Athletic Clubs, he has joined a Chinese one. Members include Indians, Tamils, Malays, Eurasians, Dutchmen, Chinese and a few Army personnel. The Club is called the “Swifts” and competing in their colours he won four cups in the Annual Singapore A.A. Championships at Jalan Besar Stadium. items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Editorial acknowledging a lean season without Surrey County titles but urging Belgravians, after the example of Frank Thomson and the club's pioneers, not to be pessimistic.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial acknowledging a lean season without Surrey County titles but urging Belgravians, after the example of Frank Thomson and the club's pioneers, not to be pessimistic. Dear Fellow Belgravians, In reading this issue it may be you will notice a slight undercurrent of melancholia. We are unable to report many successes in any section ; on the contrary, among other things, for the first time for many years, we are not now the Surrey County Champions at either Cross Country or Walking. But, do these reverses give us cause for the rumblings of pessimism we hear. Your Editors do not think so ! In our Editorials we endeavour in a few sentences to review many aspects of the Club and we feel our intended words of wisdom do much to emphasise the necessity of certain things and alternately to soothe any unwarranted apprehensions. Frank Thomson (whose obituary is published in other pages) with other pioneering Belgravians, were, in their days never deterred by pessimism, although they were up against tremendous odds. With due respect to those Belgrave stalwarts of yore, there was no possible chance to achieve anything much more ambitious than a club match win. Yet cheerfully they kept at their task and the full fruits of their endeavours were eventually realised in our many championship successes. Why, then, should we be pessimistic because we are having a few reverses ? What Frank Thomson and his colleagues did in the early days with a handful of enthusiasts we can do again, particularly with the splendid team of up-and-coming youngsters which we now have. So, away with the blues. We are still at the top of the tree in all branches of sport, the only difference being that we are sharing that position with others. Let us welcome this new state of affairs, and let it give us a greater incentive to regain our lost honours in the knowledge that it will be a much more praiseworthy achievement. YOUR EDITORS. Frank Thomson Frank Thomson pioneering Belgravian; obituary in this issue Surrey County Championships

items.label: No. 117
items.h: YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKS ON THE WINTER SEASON
items.sum: The President reflects on the club's poor winter season in open events, blaming retirements, studies and marriages, and calls for members' support to put the club back on top.
items.s: YOUR PRESIDENT SPEAKS ON THE WINTER SEASON The President reflects on the club's poor winter season in open events, blaming retirements, studies and marriages, and calls for members' support to put the club back on top. The winter season just passing has not shown the Club in a very good light as regards successes in open events. Both our runners and walkers have sadly declined in performance as reckoned on previous years, but on reading through a copy of the December, 1931, issue of the "Belgravian," I came across the following comment, which seems to me to meet the present situation :— "The true strength of any club is its numbers, enthusiasm, sportsmanship, and standard of ability, which are the true index to a club's pre-eminence, and we need have no misgivings on these points." As I stated in our last issue, we have unbounded enthusiasm as regards our Youths and Juniors, ; we also have the numbers, as witness our large fields in Club races. I do not think that anyone would question our sportsmanship, and I think our standard of ability is quite high. What, then, you may ask, is the reason for the apparent decline both in our running and walking sections ? Firstly, I think, is the inevitable retirement of some of our well-known members in both spheres, and their places are hard to fill right away, although we have the right material coming along. Then we have the numerous studies being undertaken by our members in order to help their business careers, which curtails their training time, and then we have the marriages, which are bound to come along and unless they can "school" their wives to take an interest in athletics, any time taken for training is naturally resented by their better halves ! It is rather ironic that I mentioned our cycle of successes in the last issue, but it does seem that for the moment our run of victories has been halted, although some people may think this is good for the sport as a whole. That we shall triumph again I have not the slightest doubt, but it does require the support and co-operation of all our members, which I sometimes think has been lacking in certain quarters, and let us hope that next season we shall see the "Bels" back on top once again in both the running and walking worlds. E. A. DUFFETT, President. E. A. Duffett E. A. DUFFETT President E. A. DUFFETT

items.sum: Obituary of Frank Thomson, sprinter, long-serving club official, Belgrave President and President of the Road Walking Association, who died on February 1st in his eightieth year, with a tribute from "Timber" Woodcock.
items.s: F. G. THOMSON Obituary of Frank Thomson, sprinter, long-serving club official, Belgrave President and President of the Road Walking Association, who died on February 1st in his eightieth year, with a tribute from "Timber" Woodcock. Once again the Club has suffered a very heavy blow in the death of Frank Thomson, which occurred on February 1st, in his eightieth year. Frank was not a Founder Member of the Club, but joined Belgrave—he was a Westminster resident—in its early days. He had many successes as a sprinter and, as was the custom in those days, he entered races at all distances and "had a go" at most. He played an important part in the management of the Club and in 1893 was accorded the honour of Life Membership. In 1895 he was Assistant Hon. Secretary to F. A. Bool, happily still alive and living in Chelsea, and was also a Vice-President and Hon. Auditor. In 1903 he had an operation which cut short his active career, and business and other interests claimed his attention in the years that followed. In the early 1920's Frank returned to his first love of Amateur Athletics and it is doubtful if anyone worked harder in the cause of our sport during the next twenty years. Almost every day throughout spring and summer he was at Battersea Park Track, and during the winter season he was always to be found at our mid-week quarters on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and at our Wimbledon Headquarters on Saturdays—and always working in the Club's best interests. For a while he was our Gen. Hon. Secretary, when the Club was bounding ahead, and later became Hon. Treasurer of the Surrey County A.A.A., building up the first bank balance that Association had ever known. For several years he was (jointly with F. W. Blackmore) Hon. Handicapper for Road Walking events in the south and in permanent demand as chief scoring judge at most big walking events. He was well known as a member of the Southern Committee A.A.A., and had special interests on the handicapping Board of Control. In 1935-36 Frank became President of the Road Walking Association—the first Belgrave Harrier to hold that high office. He was a Past Chairman of the R.W.A. Southern Committee and highly honoured by being elected to Life Membership of the Road Walking Association and of Les Marcheurs Francais, in tribute to his work for walking internationally. He became President of the Belgrave Harriers as the war clouds burst upon us. A partial breakdown in health in 1941 caused his retirement from business and removal to the Slough area. But still his interest in athletics persisted and he was frequently to be seen at our events. He was at our track championships last year, at the Club Dinner in October and our Open Walk in November—still showing that keenness which had always epitomised all his activities. He derived tremendous satisfaction from the Club's successes over the years with its succession of Championship titles and prominent performances, which had sprung from the few enthusiasts of the early years of the Club. Many of us will have plentiful and rewarding recollections of our old friend. We recall Frank wielding the megaphone at our track meetings, giving helpful advice to members on training nights explaining the rudiments of the Field Events and his assiduous work at our various races and on the results sheets. He will be remembered for his self-less work at some of the early Nijmegen Marches and for his hours well spent in fostering and fathering the Southern Amateur Athletic League Field Events competitions, which may truthfully be said to have been the forerunner of the greatly improved performances we see to-day. We shall remember him with the open-top bus he hired for us on Brighton Walk and Brighton Relay days ; as Trustee of the Club, conscientious and hard-working for the Club's ideals. We shall think of him, only a few months ago, with sponge and drinks at Slough Feeding Station on the Bath to London Walk, where he spent many hours helping competitors. Above all, we shall remember Frank Thomson as a great Belgravian who attained high office in the realms of athletics, yet worked effectively and unceasingly for Belgrave in fair weather and foul. Increasing years did not dull his enthusiasm, and his example is one we can all well take to heart. Frank's daughter has kindly offered us a trophy in memory of her father, and this we shall gladly accept as a perpetual reminder of one who served the Club so well and so long. R.I.P. A. A. H. Expressions of sympathy and appreciation were received from the Amateur Athletic Association, Road Walking Association, Surrey Walking Club and many who had worked with Frank over so many years. The following is an extract from a letter received from "Timber" Woodcock, Surrey W.C., and typifies the enthusiasm for our sport which Frank always showed :— ". . . I remember when I first started walking in 1930, Frank Thomson was known to me as the Southern Handicapper. In 1931, when I was a member of the Surrey Team to go to Nijmegen, I well remember that Frank was in charge of the R.W.A. Team and, with our Capt. Wilmot, he took great care of our welfare while in Holland. I remember a nine o'clock foot inspection at the end of our beds just before lights out every night. Who was first up every morning ? Why, Frank Thomson. We usually woke to find him fully dressed and having a go at those who were inclined to stop in bed at 3 a.m. Who looked after the team when on the road at check points ? Why, Frank again. And when it was all over he was the proudest man at the final ceremony when the awards were made. . . ." F. G. Thomson F. G. items.sum: Note on the illnesses of Jack Stirling Wakeley, Dick Murphy and Len Rollins.
items.s: OUR INVALIDS Note on the illnesses of Jack Stirling Wakeley, Dick Murphy and Len Rollins. Since our last issue, Jack Stirling Wakeley was taken suddenly ill and had to be rushed to hospital for an operation. We are pleased to report that he is now fully recovered and hopes to be out training again soon. Dick Murphy has been very ill, but as far as is known, he also is on the way to recovery, but has retired from business. Len Rollins, one of our very keen members in pre-war years and one who still takes a very live interest in Club activities, has also been ill. We wish both Dick and Len an early recovery. items.sum: Report of an informal meeting of about 25 runners called by Cross-Country Captain Jack Brown to discuss the section's progress, pack running, fixtures and planning for future seasons.
items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY MEETING—FEBRUARY 14th Report of an informal meeting of about 25 runners called by Cross-Country Captain Jack Brown to discuss the section's progress, pack running, fixtures and planning for future seasons. With a certain amount of trepidation, it is ventured to state that an informal meeting to discuss cross-country racing was called for the first time for some years by the Cross-Country Captain, Jack Brown. The idea basically, was to stimulate interest in winter activities and to this end two items appeared on the agenda :— 1. The progress of the Cross-Country Section this winter. 2. To discuss plans for the future. At this juncture it would probably be as well to say that there was an attendance of about 25 runners, and conspicuous by their absence were some of the great names of the Club. The meeting was opened by Denis Brickwood outlining the somewhat docile outlook of the runners to-day which had its reflection in a degree of Club stagnation. This was not to imply that we were worse than any other club—in fact, we were still more virile than most. Progress, he pointed out, could be divided into two sections : 1, The progress in ability of the individual. 2, Progress in Club outlook and spirit. He had decided that there was progress in the ability of certain runners and this implied that the training had been good. There was nothing particularly controversial about this and most speakers agreed. This naturally led to the second type of progress and Ted Stimpson, soliloquising on the past glories of the Club, said that the spirit which led them on then, was required now. Efforts had been made to get people to run in organised packs and the outcome was poor. A view was expressed that various groups did their own training which did not differ in any way from organised training. Doug Briggs and George Stace spoke most ably in their own defence, but at the same time did not disagree with the necessity for having an organised run with the pack once a week. Jack Brown, the Captain, whilst not doubting the truth of Ted Stimpson's views, ventured to say that the nature of athletics had altered in some degree and the individual performance was now considerably more important than before the war. Perhaps this was not desirable, but you had to keep pace with the times. On pack running it was explained by Denis Brickwood that it was an opportunity for the selectors to see how men were running, and this non-attendance on Saturdays had caused mistakes in selection to be made. During the season changes had been made in the organisation of packs, such as changing pace-makers periodically, but it was surprising that some members were not aware that this was being done. It had to be explained that the pack-leader ran in the body of the pack and was able to watch individual runners. The pacemakers were varied in order to afford experience and add variety to the runs. In addition, of course, it did tend to teach judgment of pace and it certainly kept the pace at a pretty high rate. To those that had not indulged in these packs, Denis Brickwood extended a cordial invitation, and assured possible clients that they would benefit from it, and even enjoy it. Passing on to the future, there was a general feeling that more thought could be given to the season before it actually started. It was conceded that the responsibility for about everything was left to Ernie Duffett, and whilst this was appreciated it did mean that, when anything was not to members' requirements, it just had to be Ernie's responsibility as no one else was involved. This was unfair and it was up to members to come forward and give their ideas to those concerned. George Chantler said that the Captains and Vice-Captains were elected to do a job and it was up to the runners to back them up. He knew the day when, if the Captain said, "We're going to run 10 miles," everyone did it. He wanted to see that once more. On fixtures, it was reported that support had been pathetic and it was lucky that there were three Bishop brothers and Bob Taylor. The average turn-out was about seven per away fixture and this was not good enough for a Club of our size. Perhaps this type of fixture was not wanted, or was it the venue ? A suggestion from Ernie Duffett was that fixtures be confined to clubs south of the Thames, and this was, in the main, agreed on by the meeting. Another point raised was the desirability of nominating the Captains well before the Cross-Country season started, so that they could take some part in making plans for the ensuing season. It was even suggested that a small Committee should be formed to properly organise the season's activities. The suggestion almost amounted to heresy in club official circles, but it was considered that it would make members more conscious of the work that was necessary in a club of our size and which was now done by a matter of half-a-dozen officials. The meeting discussed many other matters and it would take many pages to put it into print. The meeting was undoubtedly a success, and although it lasted about 1½ hours, it could have gone on much longer. It was somewhat difficult to end the meeting, but it was obvious that those who wanted to let off steam had had their chance. And now a final word to those who were not able to be present. You must have some views on cross-country running—you must have given it a thought. So, watch the notice boards, or the press, or News Letters, or this admirable magazine, for the date of the next informal meeting. items.sum: The Field Events Secretary previews the 1953 season, praises winter coaching at Battersea Park, announces entry for the Sward Trophy and urges selected members to turn up for matches.
items.s: FIELD EVENTS The Field Events Secretary previews the 1953 season, praises winter coaching at Battersea Park, announces entry for the Sward Trophy and urges selected members to turn up for matches. We are now approaching the Field Events season and I am hoping that the members of this section will get together and support George Powell, Captain, and P. Luxon, Vice-Captain. We have a very full programme, and I trust it will prove a successful one. Plaques are to be awarded, as suggested last year, for Club records. As you must know, to win one is very hard work, but it can be done and I hope 1953 will give you the opportunity. I must say that Frank Simmons and Franz Stampfl have worked hard all the winter on Saturdays and Sundays at Battersea Park, and I am sure they will be all the more pleased if their work produces good results. We have received and accepted an invitation to compete in the Sward Trophy (all field events) next May. The Club has not yet won this trophy, but we can win it if the field events men train hard enough. The events are 120 yards hurdles, 220 yards hurdles, 440 yards hurdles, 2 miles steeplechase, long jump, high jump, hop, step and jump, pole vault, discus, javelin, and hammer and shot. Entries will be sent in by the Club in April. We should very much like to cover every event, so carry on with the training and see what you can do. Further particulars can be obtained from Frank Simmons or myself. One important thing I would ask of you, and this applies equally to every member of the Club : If you are selected to represent the Club in a match, do please turn up and give us your support, or else let your Hon. Secretary or Captain know in good time so that they can fill the vacancy. Many valuable points have been lost in the past, merely because we had no one to represent us, so, whatever you do, don't let the Club down. Here's wishing you good luck and good sport. J. CHAPPELLL, Hon. Field Events Secretary. P.S.—Will any non-active members who are willing to act as officials, please get in touch with me before the track season starts ? items.s: CITY OF ROCHESTER ROAD RACE Report of the City of Rochester Road Race on November 22nd, where a below-strength Belgrave team finished 5th and Mike Stearman won the medal for first Surrey man. On November 22nd our team was decidedly below our usual strength and, in the circumstances, can be said to have done well in gaining 5th place, and they beat Aylesford Paper Mills, who won the team race last year. Our first man to finish was Mike Stearman, in 15th place, and he won a medal awarded to the first Surrey man to finish in what was quite a good class field. Thames Valley H. came along in full force and had their four scoring men in the first six places, which did not give any of the other clubs much chance in the team race. items.s: CLUB OPEN 7-MILE WALK, November 29th Report and placings of the Club Open 7-Mile Walk on November 29th, a record entry of 267, in which Belgrave were outside the prizes for the first time, Harry Churcher their first man in 6th, and Woodford Green A.C. won the Berman Trophy. Once again our Open Walk was promoted with outstanding success, that is, if we overlook the race results. Although this was Jack Goswell's first big job in his new office as Hon. Walking Secretary, he tackled it with great enthusiasm and brilliant organising ability. We thank him for his diligence in every detail and also add our thanks to Mrs. Goswell, who helped in so many ways. The prizes, as usual, were admitted by all to be grand value and were greatly appreciated by the successful competitors. As to the race itself, the results below will tell their own story, but mention must be made of the gallant effort of Harry Churcher, who was not fit, but finished in 6th position to be our first man home. Another fine performance was that of J. Haynes, who, we feel, will eventually prove a very fine team man. For the first time in the history of this race we were right outside the prize list, and this should give us food for thought as to the necessity of obtaining new blood. However, we should gain great satisfaction from the fine walking of our Juniors, particularly J. Haynes, E. Hall, and B. Eglington. items.s: "BLACKSTAFFE" SHIELD RACE Report and full results of the Club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield on Wimbledon Common on December 13th, won by Jack Brown, with the handicap and a six-a-side match against Cadogan A.C. The Club 7 miles c.c. championship was held on December 13th over our usual 2-lap course across Wimbledon Common, and although the field of 29 starters may be good by comparison with other clubs, it was a poor turn-out so far as the last two races for this trophy are concerned. Notable absentees included previous winners in Vern Blowfield and Len Herbert, and we had Eric Herbert running in the Civil Service race on the same day. Len Adams, who has recently married, and Archie Bedford, also P. G. Newell, who had been mentioned as a probable winner. Eddie Short was running for the R.A.F. in a match against the U.A.U. and Midland Counties, and Bob Taylor, who was indisposed. In mentioning the above names we are not attempting to detract from Jack Brown's running in winning the race, as his time was well up to standard and he finished in comfortable fashion in front of Chas. Walker and Bill Lucas. Mike Stearman ran well seeing that, under the new E.C.C.U. rules, he is still a junior and he pays tribute to the way he was helped along by Denis Brickwood, who seems to be regaining some of his old form. The handicap was won by George Stace, with "Jumbo" Masters in second place and Denis Brickwood third, and Masters ran very well seeing that this was his first appearance over the country this season. In a six-a-side match with our Middlesex friends, Cadogan A.C., we were easy winners and it seemed a pity that Ted Stimpson and Dick Tobin, both former stalwarts of this Club, preferred to go out for a training spin rather than run in the race. items.s: "HORWOOD CUP" 7-MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP (JUNIORS) Report and results of the Horwood Cup 7 miles junior walking championship on December 13th, won by Gerry Warr from Eric Hall and George Beecham. December 13th A good field of 20 Junior walkers, that is junior in performance, faced the starter and a very interesting race followed, with Gerry Warr and George Beecham battling all the way for first position. Eric Hall walked a very brainy race, being content to hang a little way back from the leaders. Towards the last mile George began to feel the effect of his recent foot injury and had to give way to his training comrade of their early days, thus enabling Eric to gain second place. Gerry Warr walked well and strongly right to the end and proved a worthy champion. Ted Smith had an off day, but Eglington and Ferguson showed improved form. Charlie Speechley, our evergreen at sixty-five years of age, again showed he can still show the youngsters how. We were glad to see W. Emery with us again and hope to see more of him, and L. Demmon, one of our latest acquisitions, will undoubtedly prove a useful walker with more training. Results as follows :— Handicap—1, E. Hall; 2, B. Eglington; 3, G. Warr. items.s: MATCH v. WANDSWORTH SCHOOL Report of the cross-country match against Wandsworth School at Wimbledon on 13th December, won individually by Frank Wright but lost by Belgrave on points. This was held on 13th December over our usual 3½-mile course at Wimbledon and, owing to the fact that the fixture had been arranged at the last minute, we had a job to muster a team. The School appeared to turn up in force and it was agreed to score 7 a side, which meant all our runners counting. Frank Wright was first home in the good time of 21 min. 27 secs., closely followed by Darchambaud, of the School, and this lad was at one time on our books, but has since joined South London H., and is running very well for them. A. C. McLean, our new member from the North Shields Poly., finished in 3rd place and he has shown a big improvement since he joined our ranks. J. Mitchell, 5th, and E. Cronk, 8th, also ran well, and if we had made it 4 to score we would have won with 17 points against the School's 19, but with 7 to score the points were: Wandsworth School, 49 ; Belgrave H., 56. Placings and times of our lads were—1, F. Wright, 21.27; 3, A. McLean, 22.50; 5, J. Mitchell, 23.03; 8, E. Cronk, 23.41; 14, J. Burbey, 24.45; 17, V. Taylor, 25.40; 18, J. Levene, 26.32. items.s: MATCH AT BEXLEY Report of Belgrave's one-point defeat by Cambridge Harriers in a cross-country match at Bexley on 20th December. On 20th December, against the local club, Cambridge Harriers, it was unfortunate that our captain, Jack Brown, turned up just too late to take part in the race. Holden, of Cambridge, was first home, followed by Chas. Walker, with Cass, of Cambridge, third. Then followed Bob Taylor, Denis Brickwood and J. E. Burr, but the Cambridge lads packed in well behind these and so came out winners by the narrow margine of 1 point. The course was not too well marked, and Len Bishop went off the course and this, plus Jack Brown's absence, was really responsible for us losing the match, with Cambridge scoring 40 points and ourselves 41. items.s: BOXING DAY MEETING Report of the Club's Boxing Day handicap meeting at Battersea Park, with sprint, walk, 2 miles and weight handicap results. Although the weather was not too good, a large number of Club members turned up to compete in the various events at this meeting held at Battersea Park. It was a pity that we were rather short of officials, and we do thank the few who left the comfort of their fireside to come along and help make the meeting a success. L. R. Truelove, the A.A.A. team manager, was present as a spectator and he must have been impressed not only by Jack Brown's fine running but also by the numbers present. The 120 yards Club handicap saw three heats, and those qualifying for the final were : R. Morrell (10), J. Benstead (5), C. R. Jones (11), D. Butler (6), A. Law (5), P. Cornish (6). The final saw the six runners finish almost in a straight line and the judges' placings were : 1, C. R. Jones; 2, P. Cornish ; 3, Butler. Time, 12.5 secs. The 3 miles walk handicap was won by the limit man, our old friend, Charlie Speechley, with George Oliver second, and Percy Wilson in third place. In the 2 miles run we saw the two back-markers, M. Whenman and Jack Brown, go right through their field and at the bell Jack left his pacemaker to streak ahead and win in the fast time of 9 mins. 21 secs. Eddie Paterson, off 290 yds., was second, with Whenman in third place. The Weight handicap saw a good muster of field event men, and the winner was D. Maddicks, our young javelin thrower, who, with 14ft. 6in., did 43ft. 3¾in. Frank Kemp (11ft.) was second, with Ian Forrester (16ft. 6in.) third, and the scratch man, Gaworski, did 41ft. 3¼in. L. R. items.s: COUNTY SENIOR C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS Report of the county senior cross-country championships on 3rd January: Belgrave third in the Surrey race in Richmond Park, and Cadogan A.C. sixth in the Middlesex race at Trent Park. These were held on the 3rd January, and the Surrey event was in Richmond Park, which was more or less familiar ground to our team. We were not at full strength owing to the absence of Jack Braughton, Len Herbert, Archie Bedford and Len Adams, and did not expect to retain our team title, which we had held for the past two seasons. Our team, however, all ran extremely well and we only lost first place by 5 points and second place by 1 point. Chas. Walker was our first man home in 5th position, then came Bill Lucas, 12th, and Bill only came into the team in order to make up the number, as he says he has retired from serious competition and declined an invitation to run in the Inter-Counties race. We then had three men, one behind the other, in Eddie Short 14th. Eric Herbert 15th, and Denis Brickwood 16th, and our sixth man was J. Masters 21st, and as this was the latter's first County race, he did very well and should improve with further experience. Placings and times were—5, C. W. Walker, 42.56; 12, W. E. Lucas, 44.36; 14, E. A. Short, 45.02; 15, E. Herbert, 45.05; 16, D. Brickwood, 45.06; 21, J. Masters, 45.34; 36, D. Briggs, 46.24; 44, A. H. Bishop, 47.13; 53, J. Bromley, 47.40; 55, E. M. Bishop, 47.53; 63, S. Davies, 48.36; 67, L. C. Bishop, 49.14; 74, G. J. Stace, 49.53. Team scores—1, South London H., 78 points; 3, Belgrave H., 83. The Middlesex event was held at Trent Park and here again Cadogan A.C. were weakened by the absence of Vern Blowfield, Tony Snoad, "Ginger" Newell and J. E. Burr, and were eventually placed 6th in the team race. Bob Taylor ran well to finish 20th, and Mick Porter 27th also did well, seeing that he has not done much over the country this season. Placings were—20, R. T. Taylor; 27, M. F. Porter; 63, E. Stimpson; 70, J. McDonald; 73, R. W. Tobin; 85, R. J. Wolton; 127, A. Penstone; while Ken Stimpson did not finish. It seems a pity that we cannot turn out our full-strength teams in these County races and it would seem that a bit more of the old-time enthusiasm among our members would not come amiss ! items.s: MATCH v. FINCHLEY HARRIERS Report of a cross-country match at Ruislip against Finchley Harriers and Shaftesbury Harriers, in which Belgrave were second to Shaftesbury. We were pleased to renew fixtures with this old established club, one-time National c.c. champions, but only ten of our senior members made the journey to Ruislip. Shaftesbury Harriers were also present in force and it was agreed to score 10 a side, and although we had four men in the first six home, we lost on aggregate to Shaftesbury, but managed to beat the home club. items.s: SURREY COUNTY YOUTHS C.C. RACE Report of the Surrey County Youths cross-country race staged from Belgrave Hall on 10th January, won by Frank Wright, with Belgrave taking the team title for the third year running. This was originally fixed for 6th December, but was postponed owing to fog, and we agreed to stage it in conjunction with the Junior event on 10th January from Belgrave Hall. There was a very good entry, with a field of about 100 lads, and first man home was Frank Wright in the good time of 20 mins. 57 secs. Gerry Lines gave him good support by finishing 4th, and then came J. B. Edgar, 6th, and Ron Linstead, 8th, and so we had scored our third consecutive win in this event. D. G. Hooper and J. F. Mitchell also both ran very well and we should have still won the team race with either of these counting in our scoring four. Placings and times of our lads were—1, F. J. Wright, 20.57; 4, G. At Wimbledon on 10th January there was a field of about 50 runners and, seeing that the age is 18 to 21, most of those who are eligible to run are in the Forces. items.s: "OVERSEAS CUP" RACE Report and results of the Club Youths cross-country championship for the Overseas Cup, won by Frank Wright, with the handicap won by R. J. Braine. This was the third Club Youths c.c. championship to be held for this trophy, and this year's field of 21 runners was by far the largest of the trio. Also the first three home all beat the time of 21.29 recorded by last year's winner, Geoff Goode, who is now in the Forces. In fact, all those who ran previously bettered their time this time out and this is a good sign for the future, and Mick Pyer can be well pleased with his section. Frank Wright maintained his unbeaten record over our home course, but J. B. Edgar caused a surprise by beating Gerry Lines for second place. Ron Linstead was 4th in both the scratch race also the handicap held in conjunction, but as he will still be eligible for next year's race, he should improve upon this. The handicap was won by R. J. Braine, one of our numerous members from Raynes Park County School, with M. Cunningham second, and he was making his first appearance over the country this season, and then J. F. items.s: "MACHER" SHIELD RACE Report and full results of the Macher Shield race at Wimbledon on 24th January, won by Jack Brown in 57.45, with the handicap won by Frank Mitchell. At Wimbledon, on 24th January, a field of 33 runners faced the starter, Albert Macher, and we were also pleased to see his brother, J. W. Macher, present once more. The race was two laps of our usual 5 miles course, and at the half-distance Jack Brown and Mart Whenman were running together well away from the rest of the field. We were glad to see John Bromley getting back to his old form in third place and as Whenman is only a second-claim member, and so, not eligible for a championship medal, Eddie Short took the third place award. Eric Herbert and J. E. Burr both ran well, and for the first six to finish inside 61 mins. is quite good going and compares well with previous results. The winning time of 57.45 is one of the fastest ever accomplished over this course, and both Brown and Whenman should be well up in the "National" event in March on this form. We were pleased to see Frank Mitchell win the handicap held in conjunction, a reward for perseverance, and Whenman took second prize, with J. E. Burr third. items.sum: Report and results of the Club ten mile walking championship for the Murphy Shield at Wimbledon on 24th January 1953, won by Syd James, with the handicap won by G. Warr.
items.s: CLUB TEN MILE WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP, 24th January, 1953, at Wimbledon Report and results of the Club ten mile walking championship for the Murphy Shield at Wimbledon on 24th January 1953, won by Syd James, with the handicap won by G. Warr. For holding this event the Club had decided on a new course this year, and it overcame the troubles of the past and we completed the race successfully. As the holder of this Championship was unable to walk, the Murphy Shield had a new name inscribed on it. Syd James, who has been walking well this season, carried on the good work and gained his first Club trophy. items.s: YOUTHS' ROAD TRIAL Report of the youths' road trial on 24th January to pick teams for the Aylesbury Youths Road Relay, won by Ron Linstead. This was held on 24th January with a view to selection of our teams for the Aylesbury Youths Road Relay, and a good field turned out. The course was three laps round the outside of the field at the top of Lauriston Road, and the time taken by the winner was quite good. First home was Ron Linstead, with A. C. McLean second, and Frank Wright third, and don't think Frank was trying too hard, as this was his third race in successive weeks. A new member in R. Brewer ran well, and it looks as if we have some good lads coming along to take their places in our teams for future road relays. Placings and times were—1, R. Linstead, 15.40; 2, A. C. items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Note that the junior cross-country match against Cambridge Harriers at Wimbledon on 31st December could not be held, and that only three members turned up for a senior match at Totteridge.
items.s: JUNIOR C.C. v. CAMBRIDGE H. Note that the junior cross-country match against Cambridge Harriers at Wimbledon on 31st December could not be held, and that only three members turned up for a senior match at Totteridge. This was due to be held at Wimbledon on 31st December and although about half-a-dozen of our visitors came along, including R. A. Butt, a past member of our Club, we only had one junior present, and so a race could not be held. To be fair to our lads, we must say that most of our 18 to 21 age group are doing their National Service training, and week-end leaves seem few and far between and one doubts whether it is worth while arranging such matches in future. A week later we had a senior match at Totteridge with Shaftesbury H. and T.V.H., but only three of our members turned up, and so could not count in the match, although they had a run. It does seem as if away fixtures are not welcomed by our runners and that our fixtures for next season will have to undergo a drastic alteration in make-up. R. A. Butt R. A. Butt past member of the Club; among the visitors Wimbledon Totteridge Cambridge H. Shaftesbury H. T.V.H.

items.label: No. 117
items.sum: Report of the South of Thames cross-country championship at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February, where a depleted Belgrave team was third behind Bristol A.C. and Herne Hill H.
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP Report of the South of Thames cross-country championship at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February, where a depleted Belgrave team was third behind Bristol A.C. and Herne Hill H. Held at Milford, near Godalming, on 7th February. There was a record entry of 26 teams. Clubs are only allowed to enter one team of 12 to run with 6 to score, and in the eight races since the war we have only been unplaced on two occasions and have won the team race four times. As the winning team is barred from competing again, it will be seen that fresh men have constantly to be found and we think our post-war record speaks for itself. We thought we should improve on last year's 7th position, but as we were without P. G. Newell, A. H. Bruce, B. L. Hudson, A. J. Snoad, and Mike Stearman, down with 'flu, we did not fancy our chances of getting a place. The winners of the team race were Bristol A.C., which was a just reward for their long journey, and who should be with them but our old past President, Teddy Gordon, and you can imagine his pleasure at their success and in our getting third. The individual race was won easily by "Lofty" Holden, of Cambridge H., and our first man home was Bob Taylor, 17th, our other scorers being Mick Porter, 27; John Burr, 32; Ray Tooby, 38; Len Bishop, 57, and George Stace, 61. Ray Tooby was suffering from split heels and found he could not wear his spikes and ran in rubber shoes, which no doubt was partly to blame for his backward position Our other placings were : D. Briggs, 73; J. Masters, 76 ; A. H. Bishop, 109 ; K. G. Stimpson, 111 ; E. M. Bishop, 208 ; and Eric had a pulled tendon and did well to complete the course. We were expecting Mike Stearman to arrive on the Brighton A.C. coach, but, instead, got a letter from him saying that he was down with 'flu, and this meant that we could not field a full team of 12 runners and so qualify for the "Colman" Cup, which was won by Herne Hill H. This brings up the point about all those entered who can turn out should come along with their togs in case they are required, and in any event, they can do a good job of work round the course in their track suits, as did Denis Brickwood at this race.
