items.label: No. 135
items.h: International 25 Kilometres Road Walk East Berlin Sunday May 4th
items.sum: Stan Vickers' first-person account of the trip to East Berlin for the international 25 km road walk, where he led early before fading to 12th; the walk was won by Max Weber of East Germany and the run by Kantorek, with Jack Haslam third in the run.
items.s: International 25 Kilometres Road Walk East Berlin Sunday May 4th Stan Vickers' first-person account of the trip to East Berlin for the international 25 km road walk, where he led early before fading to 12th; the walk was won by Max Weber of East Germany and the run by Kantorek, with Jack Haslam third in the run. Complete with Ted Smith's speed oil, Eric Hall's soap and Jack Goswell's map of Kent, Yours Truly, OTTO VON VICKERS set out on May 3rd for East Berlin, with long-distance runner Jack Haslam and team manager Les Truelove, for the international 25 km. run and walk. After leaving London Airport at 11 a.m. and having completed some three-quarters of our journey, Jack decided to test out the little brown bag that is so conveniently placed in front of one's seat in the aircraft.However, soon after landing a good cup of tea quickly put him on his feet again. On arriving at our hotel we had tea with our hosts, and later went out to have a look at the course, which proved to consist of a mixture of good asphalt and bad cobbles. At about 8.30 p.m. we sat down to dinner, which consisted of German sausage meat plus a famous German vegetable dish known as Sauerkraut. Haslam and Vickers, however, were not going in for this special diet so we both finished up eating Eric Hall's patent wonder food (bread and jam). We then bedded down for the night, only to discover, to our amazement, that we were without pillows. So the three happy wanderers had to be content with a tracksuit for a headrest, though this is inclined to give one a sore head on awakening. At 5 a.m. a ghastly thing called an alarm went off and Vickers got up. Now this is where I made my big mistake - if only I'd kept in bed between the sheets with my head on the hard tracksuit and my rather large feet dangling over the end of the 5 ft. long bed, I would never have taken the hiding that was forthcoming later that morning. The walk commenced at 9.30 a.m. and the field consisted of many cracks from Italy, Sweden, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Finland and West Germany. The run, which was over the same course, also attracted internationals from Poland, Czechoslovakia, Holland, Finland, West Germany and Yugoslavia and commenced at 10 a.m. It was rather a cold, windy morning when the walk started and I went off very fast, taking the lead out of the stadium after doing three and a half laps of the track. I was still in the lead at 10 km., with the two East Germans not far behind. Coming up to 12 km. we turned into a vile wind which almost picked me up and blew me off to Russia and at 14½ km. Lindner of East Germany ( a very bouncy performer indeed - he was disqualified at Melbourne for "lifting") and Max Weber also of the home country came up to my shoulder and a battle of tactics as to who should lead into the wind developed. However, the Germans soon pulled away and things remained much the same until the 20 km. check point. It was here that I received a severe shock (not an electric one) as my time was given as 89m.31s. This was incredibly fast and I found out after the race that the other competitors also felt that the sighting of this point was wrong, as indeed it must have been. From the 21 km. mark we went on to the exceedingly bad cobbles and what with these, the strong wind and my over fast start I began to feel very tired and at 22km. I was absolutely whacked. After going sprawling on the cobbles, Britain's last hope was folding up badly as one by one the opposition came past me. First there was Pamich of Italy (what a wonderful stylist he is) then Dordini (again a brilliant walker) and Soderlund of Sweden - they all went by and I couldn't do a thing about it, in fact I'd have given anything to lay down in the gutter for an hour or so. Just at that moment Dr. Pavel Kantorek, the Czechoslovakian runner,came past, followed by Paavo Kotila of Finland and our own Jackie, running brilliantly in his first international. I used my last ounce of energy to shout Jack on and then somehow managed to stagger on for a while round the lap of the stadium to finish in 12th position, a very tired young man indeed. The race was won by Max Weber of East Germany in 1hr.59m., second was Lindner of East Germany in 1hr.59m.13s. and third, A.Soderlund of Sweden in 1hr.59m.26s. After a drink of my patent pick me up (warm water), I found out that Kantorek had won the run in 1hr.20m.30s. Second was Kotila in 1hr.21m.5s., beating our Jack on the run in, his time, 1hr.21m.13s. Following a good rest in the afternoon we all went to the banquet in the evening and had a very pleasant time. After the eats and speeches, not to mention drinks, Vickers wandered off with the Dutch marathon runner Jack Smits to the hotel's "open" dance, where we had a very enjoyable time with the frauleins. All was going well until Mr Smits and myself left the hotel to walk back to our lodge when somehow or other we went off course, with the result that a fifteen minute walk took one and a half hours. We managed to find the place in the end with the help of a young German couple and such was our pleasure upon finding our home of rest that we gave them all the East German cash we had (we were leaving the following day and you cannot exchange East German marks into sterling, hence our generosity). When I entered our bedroom, Les and Jack, eyeing me with an air of suspicion, enquired where I had been. After giving my story in the utmost detail, they both told me to stop shooting a line, as they had been around etc.......etc.... If you have ever tried explaining to a team manager why you have arrived home late at night with all your money gone, you'll know what I mean! However, after promising to buy them both a drink on the following morning, the past was forgotten. A rather pleasant stay with our hosts was marred when they arrived late to take us back to the airport. After going round and round in the car for an hour ( we were trying to find the German team manager who had our visas) we eventually arrived at Temlhof Airport in Western Germany, only to find that our aircraft had left some forty-five minutes beforehand. Much good work by Les finally had us flying back via Dusseldorf and Amsterdam, to arrive at London Airport at midnight. Then came a frantic dash in Les Truelove's car. First of all he dropped Jack on his doorstep, then Stirling Fangio Truelove somehow got me to Charing Cross in time to catch the last milk train home. As you can imagine, Jack and myself were very grateful indeed, especially as Les had quite a journey to his home after dropping us. Well, the trip was over, but I think it is true to say that Jack and I had the last laugh. You see, during the outward trip we were discussing air travel, and Les told us that he could openly boast that after flying thousands of miles all over the world he had never missed an aircraft by arriving late at the airport..... ...ah well, you were saying, Mr. Truelove......? I feel sure Jack Haslam will join me in saying thank you B.A.A.B. and our German hosts for a very enjoyable trip and for the experience gained. And thankyou Les Truelove for being such a jovial and amiable team manager. Stan Vickers. items.label: No. 135
items.sum: Profile of Colin Collis, tracing his club career from joining in 1943 to his Club marathon titles, his English native record in a 3 hours track race at Walton and his retirement in 1957.
items.s: Portrait Gallery Profile of Colin Collis, tracing his club career from joining in 1943 to his Club marathon titles, his English native record in a 3 hours track race at Walton and his retirement in 1957. If perseverance, courage and fortitude can produce a self-made athlete of top class, then Colin Collis, the subject of this article, is an admirable example. He became a 'Bel' in 1943 and was a contempory of the Brown, Burfitt, Short, Adams and Bishop brothers junior group, under the eagle eyes of Bert Footer and Alf Taylor. Here he learned the true meaning of club spirit, and although he was not to come to the fore until many years later, Colin competed at all distances on the track and country. In 1951 he went to London University and there beat his head against the wall endeavouring, on the mistaken advice of a "specialist", to become a half miler, with little success. Studies kept him out of the picture for some time, but by the start of 1955 it was obvious that he had been applying himself with some diligence, to distance running, for he surprised everyone by finishing 13th in the Mitcham '15' with a time of 1hr.24m.53s. But for the fact that he had been entered in the B team and walloped several A team men, Belgrave would have been placed first. Having tasted success, Colin went on to gain fourth place in the Wigmore '15' in a very fast time, and with a second in the Surrey '20' in 1hr.47m.44s.( although, let's face it, some fantastic times are returned in this Surrey race) was a strong favourite to become Club marathon champion. This he did, in record time, when returning 2hr.37m.4s. in the Polytechnic marathon that year, at the same time winning the Lalande trophy for the first man to finish who has not competed over the distance before. Following this up with a third place in the Belgrave '20' and taking the Club title in conjunction, Colin can be said to have made a very successful entry into distance running in 1955. His meticulous attention to training and his refusal to be sidetracked from what his experience had proved to him was the best method, were to pay even greater dividends in 1956. His times were steadily improving (the greatest form of satisfaction to a road runner) and he again won the Club marathon title in record time (2hr.31m.26s.). In the Autumn of the same year Colin proved that he was really better suited to even longer distances, for he returned 3hr.2m.33s. when finishing third in the S.L.H. '30' and then received an invitation to compete in a 3 hours track race at Walton. Although suffering from a cold all the previous week, he honoured his engagement and confounded everyone by breaking the existing English native record and finishing second to the renowned Arthur Keilly of Derby. Colin covered 30 miles 952 yards 2 feet; a meritorious performance. Dogged by injury however, Colin decided to retire in 1957, temporarily we hope! He has performed official Club duties for many years and has a wise head. His compilation of Club record lists has been an interesting feature of the Belgravian since 1952. Married, with a daughter of nearly two, Colin is modesty personified, but quiet confidence always lay beneath the surface; a more purposeful athlete would be difficult to recall. items.h: Senior Match v. St. Mary's College & College of St. Mar[illegible]s and St. Johns Battersea Park 14th May.
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's senior match at Battersea Park against St. Mary's College and the College of St. Marks and St. Johns, which Belgrave won with 83 points.
items.s: Senior Match v. St. Mary's College & College of St. Mar[illegible]s and St. Johns Battersea Park 14th May. Report of Belgrave's senior match at Battersea Park against St. Mary's College and the College of St. Marks and St. Johns, which Belgrave won with 83 points. The programme for this match was restricted to five track events and three field events as the Club 7 mile walking championship, a report of which will be found elsewhere, was being held the same evening. Unfortunately, however, the start of the walk was delayed and the first track event did not take place until almost half an hour after its scheduled time. This disasterous start was somewhat remedied, so far as our guests were concerned, by the speed with which the events were carried out, and the whole evening ended on quite an amicable note. As was to be expected, with a number of first team members, we proved to be much too strong for our opponents and we provided six first and five second places. In the shorter distances our members won their respective events; Ron Holtum taking the 100 yds in 10.6s. and Brian Morris the 220 yds in 23.2s. Gerry Leroy and Henry Martin finished first and second in the 440 yds with 51.7 and 52.0s. respectively, although Gerry was rather disappointed with his performance, being hampered in training by a recurrent leg injury. Our visitors provided the winner of the 880 yds, Steve Boreham being a good second in 2m.3.2s.; he was just unable to get on terms with the winner despite his characteristic final burst. The mile proved to be an interesting race between Shipley and Len Orton, both second claim members, who finished first and second respectively in 4m.29s. and 4m.33s. Len Orton took the lead from the start, going through the three quarters quite easily,only to tire rapidly on the last lap, and he was unable to hold off Shipley's challenge about a furlong from the finish. The field events saw a welcome return to competition of Mal Ash who won the long jump with 20'6" and finished third in the javelin,with 135'5" behind Bill Couzens who threw 142'5". We also provided first place in the shot with Racey whose winning putt was 35'4". items.sum: Report of Belgrave performances in Surrey senior, junior and youths championships at Croydon Arena, led by a 4x440 yds relay win over Epsom and Ewell Harriers.
items.s: Croydon Arena May 17th Report of Belgrave performances in Surrey senior, junior and youths championships at Croydon Arena, led by a 4x440 yds relay win over Epsom and Ewell Harriers. A number of Senior and Junior championships were held in conjunction with the Surrey Youths championships and, generally speaking, those members who competed did so with distinction. Pride of place must go to our 4x440 yds Senior relay team of P.Pepe, C.Coxall, C.Jones and G.Leroy who, running in that order, defeated the holders, Epsom and Ewell Harriers, in 3m.28.3s. Pepe, running with great judgement in the outside lane, handed over with a two yard lead, after which our team were never headed and no doubt they would have beaten the existing best performance of 3m.28s. had Gerry Leroy not "coasted" during the middle part of the last lap. The same team with D.Gordon running in place of Pepe were placed third in the 4 x 110 yds relay in 45.5, despite a great effort by Charlie Jones over the last stage. Mitcham A.C. won the event in 44.2s. and Epsom and Ewell were second with 45.4s. Unfortunately our team were not awarded a set of medals as there were only five teams competing. Our two entries in the 3000 metres steeplechase, although not placed, performed most creditably, both beating time standard of 10m.15s; Clive Shippen finishing in 10m.3.6s. and Eddie Short in 10m.12s. Eddie was most disappointed with his performance, but when one considers his only training is done on the road he ran remarkably well In the junior events J.Knifton retained his title in the one mile walk in 7m.17.4s. and Alan Black, running for his school, was second to R.J.Harvey of Croydon Harriers in the one mile steeplechase. items.label: No. 135
items.sum: Unsigned training advice piece urging moderate, regular and steadily increased training rather than copying the mileage of star athletes.
items.s: Easy does it! Unsigned training advice piece urging moderate, regular and steadily increased training rather than copying the mileage of star athletes. We all know that Rome wasn't built in a day, although when the 1960 invaders have finished with it, the locals will probably wish it could be rebuilt in that time. Likewise no champion developed overnight; Sunday newspaper journalists would have us believe otherwise, but invariably omit to record the inevitable decline of these nine day wonders. The road to the top rung in athletics, let alone to the half-way rung, is a hard one, and a sensible, moderate approach to training and racing is essential if one is to avoid the disappointment of finding oneself unable to do better times in racing than in training. Of great interest to statisticians, the published questionaires answered by the stars in their various branches of athletics may well be misleading to the uninitiated, to those aspiring to fame, or to those training to a schedule which perhaps has not yet been given sufficient time to produce the required results. The mere fact that A.S.Similate thrives on 100 miles a week plus, and as a result is a likely selection for the what-have-you games, is not the slightest justification for anyone to copy him with any certain hope of success. What the questionaire probably does not state is that the subject has only arrived at his present state after years of steadily increasing the quantity and severity of his training. One man's meat being another man's poison, moderation must be practised until some indication can be obtained as to the amount of work one's body can absorb. Whatever one's event, the importance of regular training cannot be over-emphasized. Far better do little and often than two or three mammoth sessions a week. The ideal is to become as accustomed to training as one is to daily work. Look ahead, in fact look well ahead and set your sights accordingly. Make sure that you start your races with boilers at full steam, not half pressure due to injudicious training. Training will build you up - straining will break you down. Rome

items.sum: Editorial celebrating Stan Vickers' European 20 km walk gold in Stockholm and Dave Mitchell's L.C.C. Junior 880 yards win, and thanking Alf Harley for contributing much of the issue.
items.s: Editorial Editorial celebrating Stan Vickers' European 20 km walk gold in Stockholm and Dave Mitchell's L.C.C. Junior 880 yards win, and thanking Alf Harley for contributing much of the issue. Dear Fellow Members, We are indeed proud to record the outstanding achievement of Stan Vickers in outclassing the best walkers in Europe to win the gold medal at Stockholm in the European 20 kilos. Championship. For this superb performance Stan has been awarded the "Tommy Green" trophy; it was never more gallantly earned. Since our last edition great improvements have been shewn in our track performances, the most notable being that of Dave Mitchell when winning the L.C.C. Junior 880 yards Championship in 1m.57.8s; a remarkable time for a junior. We hope Dave turns out to be a future middle distance star. We are indebted to Alf Harley for much of the material contained in this issue, but it is regrettable that one on whose shoulders rests so much responsibility on behalf of the Club, should have need to add to his duties by writing articles for this magazine. If one who is so fully occupied already can find time to do this, then we hope others will feel how small is their own contribution to the running of a Club as large as ours. Stan Vickers Stan Vickers won gold, European 20 km walk, Stockholm; awarded the "Tommy Green" trophy Stan Stan Dave Mitchell Dave Mitchell won L.C.C. items.sum: New club president F.R. Webb thanks members for electing him, asks for regular training to put the club back on top, and congratulates European champion Stan Vickers.
items.s: From your President New club president F.R. Webb thanks members for electing him, asks for regular training to put the club back on top, and congratulates European champion Stan Vickers. Fellow Members, I should like to take this opportunity, through the medium of the Belgravian, to express my sincere thanks for the great honour you have paid me by electing me as your President, and I shall do all in my power to carry out the duties involved to the best of my ability. It is my hope that during the next twelve months I shall have the help of all members in putting the Club back on top, where it belongs, and this can only be done by regular training with the various packs which will be arranged by your Cross-Country Captain. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate our European Champion, Stan Vickers, on his great walking performances during the past season. Once again thanking you all very much for this honour. F.R. Webb F.R. Webb F.R. Webb President Stan Vickers Stan Vickers European Champion (walking) European Championships

Socially Speaking..... On taking over the Office of Social Secretary I would like to say a few words and to ask you for your support at all social functions during the coming year. No matter how much time and hard work is put into the arrangement of a social function such as a Dance, Dinner or Coaches for the Brighton Relay etc., it cannot be a success without your full support and encouragement. So come along and enjoy the companionship of fellow Belgravians. Social Dances Social Dances at Belgrave Hall have been arranged to take place approximately once a month, the first being on October 25th and the last in March. A licensed bar will be available on each occasion and a first class band will be engaged. Refreshments at moderate prices will also be obtainable. Games will be organised and there will be spot prizes to be won. Sausage and Mash Supper It is hoped to have a sausage and mash supper available to members and their friends after the afternoon's activities on the days of socials and dances. A list will be posted on the notice board at the hall two or three weeks before each dance and you can assist us a great deal by placing your name thereon and indicating how many persons will be making up your party. This will greatly assist us in knowing how many to cater for. Tooting Bec gave us every encouragement on our return to its track by welcoming us with a lovely day and beautiful sunshine, bringing out our feminine admirers in all their bright best and enabling our noble band of officials to display themselves without jackets in impeccable whiteness in accordance with the well known advertisements. Outstanding amongst these were the doubles of Clive Ryan in the 100 and 220 yds. and John Davies in the 880yds and 1 mile. The forward running of R. items.sum: Obituary of race walker Bert Clayton, who died aged 39, recalling his Horwood Cup win, R.W.A. team placings, 50 km championship medals and Nijmegen Shield wins.
items.s: H.G. Clayton Obituary of race walker Bert Clayton, who died aged 39, recalling his Horwood Cup win, R.W.A. team placings, 50 km championship medals and Nijmegen Shield wins. It is with sincere regret that we record the passing of Bert Clayton at the early age of 39 years; and our heartfelt sympathy is extended to his Wife and three children. Bert joined us in 1938 and in that year won the Horwood Cup Championship. In the early part of 1939 he was a member of our winning R.W.A. Junior Championship team at Manchester; and a few weeks later figured prominently in the R.W.A. 20 miles Championship at Mill Hill. In this he was nominated as a "B" team man but was able to assist our fourth "A" team man, Harry Thaxter, to complete a Belgrave team win; and was content to finish in 17th position himself, following Thaxter in. During the war Bert served in the R.A.F. but in 1947 was again assisting our teams. He was in our 'placed' R.W.A. 20 miles teams in 1947-48-49-50 and in our winning team at Enfield in 1952. He was placed third in the R.W.A. 50 kilometres Championship at Sheffield in 1950 ( when our team was second) and second the following year at Brighton when we were the Championship winners. Bert won our Club 20 miles Championship in 1950 and 1951; and scored in our winning Nijmegen Shield teams in 1948, 1950 and 1952. It will be seen from the foregoing that Bert was a great team walker; and in addition to the strength he brought to our Championship teams he was a valuable team man in other events also. Living at Eastleigh, he travelled considerable distances for his racing, but always did so cheerfully and enthusiastically and endeared himself to a very wide circle of friends. We have lost a great sportsman and a great Belgravian - we are the richer for having known him so well, the poorer for his passing from our midst. A.A.H. H.G. Clayton H.G. items.sum: Report and results of the R.W.A. 50 km walk championship held from Belgrave's headquarters, won in a British fastest time by Metropolitan's D.J. Thompson, with Eric Hall third and Belgrave winning the team title for the third successive time.
items.s: The R.W.A. 50 kilometres Championship Report and results of the R.W.A. 50 km walk championship held from Belgrave's headquarters, won in a British fastest time by Metropolitan's D.J. Thompson, with Eric Hall third and Belgrave winning the team title for the third successive time. For the first time ever this Championship was held from our Headquarters and our thanks from the Club are due to all those who helped with the organisation of the race, which reflected great credit on Belgrave. Jack Goswell and Arthur Whitehead were, as usual, in the forefront of the arrangements but there were many others who gave assistance and made this a memorable Championship from the organisation point of view. The course consisted of five laps of the approximately one mile lap of the Common at the head of Lauriston Road, followed by four laps of our normal course ( of 6 miles 1114 yards each) taking in Park Side, Tibbetts Corner, Robin Hood Way, Coombe Lane, Copse Hill and finishing at Lauriston House There were 96 starters and [illegible]ric Hall was soon prominent among the leaders and, in fact, held the lead for a while soon after the 20 kilometres mark. At half-distance Misson(Met.W.C.) had taken the lead with Johnson(Sheffield) near at hand followed by Don Thompson(Met) and Eric, taking things reasonably easy, fourth. A few kilometres later Thompson went into the lead and rapidly went away from the field to record the fastest time yet over the 50 kilometres distance in this country. Misson whilst not quite so fast as his club mate also forged away from the field, and Eric Hall took over third position from a tiring Johnson, who was also experiencing foot trouble. Eric, realising the impossibility of cutting into the lead of the two Metropolitan walkers ahead of him, was well content with his position and the excellent start it gave to our team in their efforts to retain the Championship title. Metropolitan succeeded in taking fourth individual place with Nigel Thompson, thus having three men in the first four, but adequate backing for them was missing. Eventually their fourth man finished in 41st scoring position. Our strength is, of course, in numbers and solid team work and this was well exemplified by our supporting walkers. George Checkley did not have one of his happiest races, yet stuck to his task and, walking a tremendously fast last lap, finished in eighth position. Ray Hall started well and finished well, but there were times in between when he was very far from happy. His ninth position was of the greatest value to the team; and we are all confident that he will be a "placed" man at this distance one day. Our team was completed by Hugh McGreechan, in twelfth position, who walked a typically sound race. Four men in twelve is normally good enough to win a Championship and so it was, and our third successive win was accomplished. Near at hand was George Beecham (17th) to take over, should it become necessary. To conclude, we may derive great pleasure from this further Championship win, from the success which attended our organisation of the Championship entrusted to us and in Eric Hall's third placing which confirmed the extreme versatility and excellence of his walking at varying distances. items.sum: Report on Belgrave performances at Herne Hill Harriers' Brockman Trophy meeting, with wins for Percy Porter (hammer) and Norman Caves (hop, step and jump), seconds for John Davies and Pat Newell, and sixth place overall for the club.
items.s: Brockman Trophy Meeting 7th June Report on Belgrave performances at Herne Hill Harriers' Brockman Trophy meeting, with wins for Percy Porter (hammer) and Norman Caves (hop, step and jump), seconds for John Davies and Pat Newell, and sixth place overall for the club. Organised by Herne Hill Harriers, this meeting is always very hotly contested, and in consequence the standard of performance is particularly high. Although our field events representatives were few in number they certainly made their presence felt and in the very first event, the hammer throw, Percy Porter won with a throw of 157'5". Norman Caves won the hop, step and jump with 43'3" while in the pole vault Mal Ash did well to secure fourth place. Our track runners were more numerous, although in some of the events they were completely outclassed, notably the 880 yds, in which P. Pepe was unable to qualify for the final, and the 6 miles in which Eric Gebbett finished sixth. However, John Davies and Pat Newell came to the rescue with two very fine efforts, John finishing second to Gordon Pirie in the 1500 metres with a time of 3m.59 1s. and Pat chased John Disley home in the 3 miles to finish less than two seconds behind in 14m.39 6s. and incidently beat Langridge of S.L.H. who is no mean performer. Clive Shippen, our budding steeplechase star, was third in the 3000 metres event with a time of 10m.12s. Mal Ash was unluckly not to qualify in his heat of the 120 yds hurdles which was won in a very fast time while C.R. Jones ran into fourth place in the 220 yds final. In the 4 x 440 yds relay our quartet were fourth, behind Blackheath, London A.C. and T.V.H. Our final place in the contest was sixth. items.sum: Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon from Windsor to Chiswick, incorporating the A.A.A. and Southern marathon championships, where Len Bishop retained the club title in a club record and Belgrave won the Southern team title.
items.s: Polytechnic Marathon and Club Championship Report and results of the Polytechnic Marathon from Windsor to Chiswick, incorporating the A.A.A. and Southern marathon championships, where Len Bishop retained the club title in a club record and Belgrave won the Southern team title. One hundred and ninety-four runners set out from Windsor Castle on the afternoon of June 28th for the annual dash to Chiswick via the country lanes of Berkshire and Buckingham. Incorporated in the event this year were the A.A.A. and Southern Counties Marathon Championships and an additional attraction was the possibility of a trip to either Cardiff or Stockholm. With the Club Championship his target, Eric Gebbett led the Belgrave contingent of nine runners for the first sixteen miles, which he covered in the rather fast time of 89m.25s. Shortly after this point he was overtaken by Len Bishop, the Club title holder, who was determined that his title would not be relinquished at any price. Eric hung on desperately for the next three miles, but Len's fighting qualities were never more in evidence than now, as he began to draw steadily away. Len eventually finished 13th in the new Club record time of 2h.30m.39s. and in fact was actually on the track at the same time as such distinguished marathon runners as E.L. Smith of Leeds and F. Norris of Bolton. Eric, in finishing 17th performed extremely well, and was comfortably inside the A.A.A. standard of 2h.35m. The third Club runner to finish was Bob Plummer, who recorded his best ever time of 2h.36m.46s. to occupy 25th position. Bob has now regained the excellent form he was showing two years ago when he was laid low by a very troublesome knee injury. The efforts of these three stalwarts won us the Southern A.A.A. Marathon team Championship which we last held in 1955. Nearly ten minutes were to elapse before our next man, Geoff Pearson, put in an appearance, and his running enabled us to secure third place in the Open Team Race. Geoff doesn't turn out for the Club very often now but when he does he can always be relied upon to put up a stirling performance. Our four remaining runners all completed the course, and special mention must be made of the running of J. MacDonald who was expected by many to be well outside three hours but in actual fact beat the new Club Standard of 2h.55m. We had a fairly good turn out of Seniors for this match which was a four sided affair against Victoria Park, Deptford Park and Ilford A.C. but our Junior representation consisted of only one person. As the match was to be decided on the total number of points, both Senior and Junior, this placed us at a very great disadvantage. So much so, that in spite of winning seven Senior events we lost the match. John Davies won both the half and one mile in 1m.57 6s. and 4m.23s. respectively, while Brian Morris had a narrow win in the 220 with a time of 22 7s. There were two races over 440 yds, Charlie Jones being second (52 4) in the first one and Alan Jackson winning the second in 52 6 Dave Ansell won the 100 yds in 10 8s. and the long jump with 20'7". The match resulted in a win for Victoria Park with 104 pts. Ilford A.C. were second with 96, ourselves third with 80 and Deptford Park fourth with 71. John Davies John Davies won half mile 1m.57 6s. and mile 4m.23s. Brian Morris Brian Morris won 220 yds 22 7s. items.s: PETERBOROUGH MARATHON JULY 19TH Report of the Peterborough Marathon run in heat with Belgrave runners placed and Belgrave second team behind Leeds Harehills. Support for this race has, in the past, been very poor, but this year saw a vast improvement with an entry of over eighty of whom sixty-four actually started. Despite this large entry the promoters only saw fit to give one set of team prizes although in fairness to them this fact was advertised freely before the race. However, one would have thought that this unexpectedly heavy support would have made them change their minds. The rather slow times were due to the fact that the race was run throughout in blazing sunshine and with a temperature of 84 degrees. 10,R. Plummer 2h.55m.54s; 13, H.A. Bishop 3h.00m.18s; 22, J. items.s: INTER-CLUB MATCH AT CHARLTON PARK JULY 26TH Report of a triangular match with Cambridge Harriers and Herne Hill Harriers at Charlton Park, won by Belgrave seniors while the juniors finished third. This was a triangular affair involving ourselves, Cambridge Harriers and Herne Hill Harriers and once again John Davies won both the 880 yds. and 1 mile although the times were only moderate. Charlie Jones won both sprints in 10.2 and 23.0 and also the high jump with 5'2". Len Orton was well beaten by J. Heywood of Herne Hill in the 3 miles, Len's time being 15m4s. In the shot and discus we didn't fare too well, collecting only 8 points to the Hill's 20 and Cambridge's 14. The 440 yds. was easily won by Alan Jackson in 52.6, the second man being timed at 55.4. We defeated Cambridge in the 4 x 110 yds relay, 45.4 to 46.8. Senior match result:- Belgrave 74; Cambridge 60; Herne Hill 58. Our Juniors were heavily defeated in their match and in fact only won one event, the mile, in which D. Crookes returned 4m.38.2s. Eric Penny was third in the 440 yds and his time was 57.8s. Junior match result:- Herne Hill 77; Cambridge 74; Belgrave 38. There was a very good turn out of both Juniors and Seniors for this mid-week fixture which, however, resulted in a win for Sutton and Cheam with 69 pts. to our 53. items.h: BELGRAVE OPEN 20 MILES RUN AND CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP AUG.16TH
items.sum: Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 miles, where Len Bishop finished third and won the club championship in a club best championship time, and Belgrave A were second team to Thames Valley Harriers.
items.s: BELGRAVE OPEN 20 MILES RUN AND CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP AUG.16TH Report and results of the Belgrave Open 20 miles, where Len Bishop finished third and won the club championship in a club best championship time, and Belgrave A were second team to Thames Valley Harriers. A smaller than usual field of 83 was sent on its way by the Deputy Mayor of Wimbledon in weather which, for a change, was not of the heat wave variety. In fact, conditions could be described as near perfect. Belgrave's contribution to this field consisted of two teams of six runners each. Eric Gebbett was the early pacemaker from Beale of Shaftsbury and at twelve miles he was passed by Haslam(T.V.H.) and Salvat(Finchley). Len Bishop, who had been content to hang back in the early stages, now began to move up and at sixteen miles passed Eric at great speed. Maintaining his speed to the end of the race he finished a very good third in the Open Race and was a comfortable winner of the Club Championship. Eric, although taken aback by this burst of speed was still an easy fourth, exactly two minutes ahead of the next man, Harry Dennis of T.V.H. With Bob Plummer running well for twelfth place our team was narrowly beaten by T.V.H. Mention must be made of Ron Linstead and Joe Dooley, who were running in their first 20 mile race. To beat 2h.5m. on this course was a particularly good effort. Once again Bill Bird and Arthur Whitehead plus their numerous assistants must be congratulated for the way the race was organised. The winning time was a new Club best Championship performance. Also started:- K. Stimpson and J. Baker. Standards (2h.15m.) J. Dooley, R. Linstead, G. Pearson, H.A. Bishop, J. McDonald 3 L.C. items.sum: Report of a small Belgrave team's successful visit to a minor meeting on a muddy grass track at Bishop's Stortford, winning the 440 yds, 220 yds and 4 x 440 relay.
items.s: Report of a small Belgrave team's successful visit to a minor meeting on a muddy grass track at Bishop's Stortford, winning the 440 yds, 220 yds and 4 x 440 relay. On Saturday Sept.20th a small team visited Bishop's Stortford on a minor "pot hunt" with considerable success. The grass track was very soggy and in some parts was just plain muddy. Hence the rather slow times. In the 100 yds. heats our only competitor, C.R. Jones, came through at about 75 yds. and won easily in 10.5s. Starting much faster in the final (from borrowed blocks) he was only inches down on the leader at 50 yds. Everyone, including the official winner, thought he had won with his dip finish, but the judges deemed otherwise and he was given second place. Times (non electrical) 10.7 & 10.8. The 220 yds heats went off uneventfully with Brian Morris and Charlie Jones qualifying easily for the final. The next event concerning the Bels was the 440 yds which was run as a straight final, and taking part was our 4 x 440 relay team. Alan Jackson and P. Pepe started rather fast into the mud while Brian Morris and Frank Wright went off steadily. At the half-way mark Brian was leading slightly from Frank, but Pepe and "Jacko" found the heavy grass track not to their liking and decided to save their energies for the relay. Brian and Frank continued running very strongly and drew away from the field to finish first and second in 51.4 and 51.6 respectively. Twenty-five minutes later came the 220 final. Charlie,in the fourth lane, started well, catching Brian coming off the bend and holding his lead to the finish. Brian, although feeling tired after his "quarter", finished close up in second place, giving the Bels another maximum. Time 23s.? The "quarter" men next performed as a team in the 4 x 440 relay and showed their superiority by finishing more strongly than their opponents who, however, put up quite a fight. Belgrave first again, time 3m32s. The team then headed back to civilization in cars, motor-bikes and scooters. C.R. Jones C.R. items.label: No. 136
items.h: Some notes on the A.G.M. Sept.25th.
items.sum: Wry account of the club's Annual General Meeting, covering the Hon. Secretary's report, interruptions from members, elections and Charlie Munro's election to Life Membership.
items.s: Some notes on the A.G.M. Sept.25th. Wry account of the club's Annual General Meeting, covering the Hon. Secretary's report, interruptions from members, elections and Charlie Munro's election to Life Membership. The A.G.M. opened (apart from the reading of previous minutes and noting apologies from absentees) with the Hon. Secretary's Report from which we were encouraged to learn that apart from a temporary setback in cross country and middle distance running (formerly our main strength) we nevertheless had reason to be proud of the Club's overall contribution to the sport. Thanks to our walkers and late season form of our track relay men, our record last year was quite a good one. The adoption of this report was temporarily delayed by the snarling interruption of a rather incoherent member who seemed rather concerned that a first claim Belgravian had competed for another club. He quickly subsided - still muttering - on learning that his outburst was out of order at that stage. We were then taken through the accounts and there followed the usual rather dry proceedings until we came to the election of officers, and this was marked by the efforts of current holders of office to transfer their mantels to other shoulders. We learned, among other things, that while the job of auditing the Club books was small, the journey from Chislehurst to Edmonton was long. This piece of information prompted a former Hon. Treasurer to jump to his feet and to question whether the audit had been properly carried out. His feigned criticism was an attempt to inject a note of humour into the otherwise rather dull proceedings, but he was perhaps rather unwise in attempting to draw a comparison between the somewhat more arduous and complicated accounting of his day with that at present obtaining. This brought quite a storm about his head from the platform, and whilst this forced him to hastily resume his seat with apology, he was re-assured by the accompanying applause that not all members were devoid of a sense of humour. The election of a new committee followed uneventfully and it was not until "any other business" that the meeting once more briefly came to life. Again it was the incoherent member who seemed anxious to repeat his previous uninformed comments regarding the first claim Belgravian, and went on to discuss the merits of our distance runners generally and our 3 and 6 milers in particular. Whilst most of this was rather incomprehensible, one could not escape the impression that the speaker was not altogether satisfied with their performances, but before he got very far, another member interrupted - rather violently it was thought - to discuss, not athletics, but some sort of ball game. It was all very bewildering. The meeting ended having elected, among others, a new President, a new cross country caption, a new social secretary, a new committee, but not a new junior section secretary, probably the most important job of them all. Charlie Munro was elected to Life Membership. One came away from the meeting with the feeling that without the presence of the General Hon. Sec. the A.G.M. could well have got out of hand. He has held this post for a long time and while he repeatedly expresses the view that a younger member should be considered to take over this important job, it is evident, that for the present at least, there is no one of sufficient stature to replace him. Charlie Munro Charlie Munro elected to Life Membership A.G.M. Chislehurst Edmonton

items.s: A few words from your Track Hon. Secretary The Track Hon. Secretary looks ahead to the 1959 season, asks for more support from distance runners and thanks second-claim member Len Orton, who is returning to Birchfield. I look forward to the 1959 season with confidence and the expectation that our teams will be much stronger in all departments. Particularly would I like to see more support from our two and three milers. This year we have missed the assistance of Chas. Walker, Dave Baulch, Brian Hallowell and others. We must thank our second claim member, Len Orton, for his support at our fixtures. I understand that he will be returning to his first claim club Birchfield very soon and I feel sure that he carries our best wishes for his future, both in his athletics and his career. D.M.S. D.M.S. items.s: CLUB 5[illegible] MILES ROAD RACE SEPT 27TH Report and results of the club road race over the Common, won comfortably by Pat Newell, with Clive Shippen second, Ken Stimpson winning the handicap, and a plea for winter cross-country training. A spectacular return to form by Charlie Dabbs, a defiant battle against "father time" and injuries successfully overcome by Archie Bedford, and an extraordinary run by Clive Shippen were just a few of the highlights to emerge from this event, considered by some to be an unofficial "Brighton" trial. With so little having been seen of our key road-relay men this summer there was considerable speculation as to how they would fare against the fitness of the long distance men and the speed of the middle distance track runners on this both tough and fast course. To add to the uncertainty Archie Bedford and Len Adams were reputed to be making a determined effort to regain their long lost places in the London-Brighton relay team. So, on a fine day and in ideal conditions, our new President, Frank Webb, sent the 40 odd runners on their way. After one lap of the Common very little had been decided despite the faster than usual start; Pat Newell slightly led a pack of about eight runners, with a few more in close attendance. No sooner had the second lap commenced than Pat decided to increase the tempo, only Dave Baulch attempting to go with him. However,on leaving the Common for Copse Hill Pat was way ahead and increasing his lead with every stride; the role of pack leader being taken over by Eric Gebbett. On entering Cambridge Road with the hills still to come this group had been reduced to Gebbett, Walker, Baulch, Robinson and Shippen. Dave dropped back at the approach to the first hill and Malcolm likewise at the turn into the second; the remaining three staying together until approximately 400 yds. to go when Clive Shippen sprinted ahead to gain second place, 25 yds. ahead of Charlie Walker, with Eric a further 35 yds. down. Charlie Dabbs proved his unexpected fitness by finishing strongly, only 10 sec. behind Gebbett. Pat Newell must be congratulated on his fine solo effort; he ran comfortably throughout and was at no time fully extended. Bob Glover ran in this event for the first time last March when he returned a time of 30.35. His time today? 29.38! Establishing himself as a runner of note in such a short time makes one wonder how much potential he has yet to realise. Special mention should also be made of Archie Bedford on his most welcome return to form, and of a fine performance by young Radford. The handicap was won by Ken Stimpson who produced a time considerably faster than his usual. Second place went to Glover and a deserved third to Dennis Jones who is running better than ever before. Once more we are on the brink of another winter season and if all of today's competitors take an active part in the programme, it should be a successful one; and 1959 could take us out of the "fifties" on the same triumphant note with which we entered them nearly ten seasons ago. Belgrave possesses almost unlimited depth but, as yet, no stars. An enthusiastic winter season could well remedy this weakness. To those who are dubious of working hard over the country it might well be worth mentioning names like Herb Elliott, Derek Ibbottson and John Merriman. Ibbottson's "failure" this season followed a winter of negligible cross-country work, whereas his triumphant summer of 1957 was produced by a winter in which he won major international cross-country races during an extremely active season. items.sum: Report of the Road Runners Club London to Brighton run, where Bob Plummer was tenth with a first class standard and Belgrave's four runners took third team prizes behind T.V.H. and Derby and County.
items.s: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RUN, SEPT. 27TH. Report of the Road Runners Club London to Brighton run, where Bob Plummer was tenth with a first class standard and Belgrave's four runners took third team prizes behind T.V.H. and Derby and County. (Promoted by the Road Runners Club) On the first stroke of seven, some forty-eight runners, including four Belgravians, started from Westminster. The weather, a little cold and damp at the start, developed into a good day for this type of race. At five miles our four, Alan Bishop, Joe MacDonald, Bob Plummer and Wally Wortley were running together at just inside seven minutes a mile. At ten miles Bob was nearly a minute ahead of our other three who came through steadily. The next ten miles on towards Redhill saw Bob still running strongly whilst our others had spread themselves out a little, the order being Wally, Alan and Mac.Times of our runners at 20 miles:- Bob(2h.15m.27s.),Wally (2.22.28.), Alan(2.22.38.) and Mac(2.22.53.). At thirty miles Wally had some trouble with his back and stopped for a while and was passed by Alan and Mac, Alan having a lead of over four minutes on Mac. On to Handcross, with eighteen miles still to go, Bob was still going well and Wally was losing ground to Mac. The road after Handcross, in spite of its downward trend,has often troubled the best and Bob and Alan both had bad patches along this stretch. Alan told me afterwards that he was short of training and in consequence he had several miles of slow running. So to the finish, Bob Plummer, full of running again, was tenth in 6h.22m.2s., his best ever with a First Class Standard. The team race (3 to score) was already won by T.V.H. with fourteen points, but we had hopes of a place. Wally Wortley, who was still three minutes behind Mac. at Pyecombe and had passed Alan two or three miles back, had made a grand recovery and finished strongly in fifteenth position with a time of 7h.00m.33s. Joe MacDonald was next man in in 7h.02m.53s, he had had a hard run over the last few miles and seemed very glad to finish. Our team was in with 31 points, but Derby & County and Orion had two men well placed and could still beat us. Derby's third man made their score 22 points, so it was Belgrave or Orion for third place. Meanwhile Alan Bishop had finished nineteenth in 7h.15m.39s. and although not scoring added a point to the Orion score which, when their third man did arrive, equalled our own. With our third man in front of Orion's third man we were awarded the third team prizes. Alan was not unrewarded, as he gained a Second Class Standard as did Wally and Mac. The day was rounded off by having tea with the Mayor of Brighton (who has threatened to run in next years' race) and the presentation of well earned awards. G.D. Crawley 30.6m. Handcross 35.1m. items.label: No. 136
items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes: Ted Good's recovery and club history since 1897, Eric Hall's walking record in 1958, John Sams's hurdles titles, Dave Mitchell, the W.J. Pepper Memorial Cup, relay finals, John Palmer's illness, and Stan Vickers's Tommy Green Cup with Harold Whitlock's praise of his European Games walk win.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S CORNER The Hon. Secretary's notes: Ted Good's recovery and club history since 1897, Eric Hall's walking record in 1958, John Sams's hurdles titles, Dave Mitchell, the W.J. Pepper Memorial Cup, relay finals, John Palmer's illness, and Stan Vickers's Tommy Green Cup with Harold Whitlock's praise of his European Games walk win. We congratulate Ted Good on recovering from a very serious illness and wish him well for many years yet. Ted was sustained in his battle for life by the fighting spirit he acquired fifty years earlier in the Club teams and, he writes, in his delirious condition he re-fought his team battles over and over again and they gave him the desire and strength to win through, and satisfy his doctors. Ted joined the Club in 1897. He was then a young man who listened to his foreman (a Belgrave Hon. Secretary) talking of sporting walkers at lunch time, and enquired how he could join Belgrave. He was told that the first step was to sign a nomination form and submit it with a shilling entry fee. To do this, Ted who lived at Chelsea and worked at Baker Street, got up earlier each morning and walked to work, thus saving the two-pence a day allowed him by his mother for workman's fare. Thus in a week he saved his nomination fee and became a member in 1897 ( when his wages were 10/- weekly for a sixty-hour week! ), and was elected to Life Membership 54 years ago. Ted Good, who was an Hon. Editor in 1908, now lives at Brighton; and weather permitting, tries to get to the finish of all the big athletic events in the hopes of seeing a Belgrave win. Eric Hall's versatility as a walker can never have been surpassed in the history of the sport; and his record in 1958 of not having been further back than fifth in any of the five major championships ( three on the road and two on the track) must be unique. The performances are :- What a magnificent record! Our heartiest congratulations go to John Sams on winning the A.A.A. and Southern 200 yards Hurdles Championships, and the L.C.C. junior 100 yards Championship. John may be booked for the Army soon but we look forward to seeing him in our senior teams in the years ahead, and have every confidence that his ambition to win an A.A.A. 440 yards Hurdles Championship will be realised one day. Another junior whose future looks bright is Dave Mitchell who put up a personal best time in winning the L.C.C. Junior Half Mile Championship very cleverly from a good class field. We derived a great deal of pleasure in winning the "W.J.Pepper Memorial Cup" for the Club gaining the greatest aggregate of points in the L.C.C. Championships; for Bill Pepper had very close associations with our Club going back many years. Our former President, Bob Ricketts and Bill were great friends, and Bill always had a very warm spot in his very warm heart for Belgrave. We were also pleased in the manner of winning, for our Runners, Field Events men, Walkers and Juniors all shared in the effort - which is Club spirit at its best. There was also pleasure in seeing our teams finish second and fourth respectively in the 4 x 110 yards and 4 x 440 yards A.A.A. Relay Championships. Only two clubs could qualify for both finals, and we were one of them! John Palmer has resumed light training and we would hope that perhaps in twelve months time he will be claiming a place in our teams. After showing great promise as a Junior, John did his National Service with the Army in Germany, where he had many close races with J. Merriman who has subsequently distinguished himself both on track and cross-country in the highest company. Most unfortunately, John Palmer was found to have a kidney complaint on his return to civil life, and this has necessitated long treatment which appears to have been successful, as was forecast. Meanwhile every time Merriman runs it serves to underline the potentialities of our John Palmer; and we hope his cure will be complete and permanent. The "Tommy Green" Cup for the best athletic performance of the year by a Club member has been awarded to Stan Vickers for his magnificent win in the 20,000 metres European Games Walk. Could there be any argument? The following comments from Harold Whitlock, a former Olympic and European Games Champion himself, who acted as Chief Walking Judge at Stockholm will be read with pride by all Belgravians. "I arrived back with the British Team last evening after a good week in Stockholm. The team was one of the happiest that have taken part in any of these events. That was the opinion of the athletes themselves, and much of the credit must go to the officials with the team for their handling of the group. Without doubt the Team's success sprung from the inspiration given them by Stan Vickers, whose performance was the best piece of race-walking I have ever seen. He was always the master, even when behind the leaders in the initial stages, and when he decided to go they just could not match him, and in trying to do so two of them suffered disqualification. Belgrave have good reason to be very proud of Stan and I can tell you that I, too, felt very proud when the judges congratulated me on his success and said that he was without doubt the best walker in every respect. As an Ambassador of British walking he is likely to open up avenues that have eluded us in the past, such is his prestige among the walking nations". items.sum: New-year editorial urging members to support the club and train harder, singling out junior C. Thompson as a promising athlete.
items.s: EDITORIAL New-year editorial urging members to support the club and train harder, singling out junior C. Thompson as a promising athlete. Dear Fellow Members, Although a little late, we take this opportunity of wishing all members a happy and successful new year. Doubtless many resolutions have already suffered their inevitable fate, but at least two should still be foremost in our minds. Firstly let us resolve to support our Club in as many events as possible, whether as competitors or officials and secondly,we must resolve to train harder, this applies especially to our youths and juniors. The amount of punishment a properly trained athlete can absorb is fantastic. If we remember that most fatigue is purely psychological, then perhaps we can drag ourselves out for that training session which, although dreaded, invariably becomes most enjoyable. Certain members stand out as likely to perform exceptionally well in Belgrave colours this year, and among them is C. Thompson, a junior, whose improvement during the last year has been great to see. He has a fine future ahead of him provided he is able to distinguish between good and bad advice as regards his training and choice of events. It is a pity that so much harmful advice is often given to young athletes when their careers are in the infancy stage. C. Thompson C. Thompson junior, praised for improvement

items.s: TED GOOD Obituary of Ted Good, a member for over half a century, who died after a serious illness. In our last issue we gave news of Ted Good, whose years with the Club extended over half a century. We now learn with sincere regret of his death; it is evident that he never fully recovered from his most serious illness of a few months ago. Ted's passing means the severing of yet another link with our early history and it is pleasing to note that he was so recently able to put into proper perspective, for many of us, the early days of the Belgrave Harriers and those who made up the Club in those days. Our sincere sympathy goes to Ted's widow. A.A.H. Ted Good Ted Good death; member for over half a century A.A.H. A.A.H.

items.sum: Obituary of George Still, a familiar club figure for sixty years and former Highgate Harriers runner, who died aged 82 after swimming.
items.s: George Still Obituary of George Still, a familiar club figure for sixty years and former Highgate Harriers runner, who died aged 82 after swimming. We mourn the passing of one who had been a familure figure in the Club dressing rooms and over our courses for sixty years and more. Many of us had our first run over Wimbledon Common with George, and listened to his reminiscences of races and athletics of years gone by with glowing interest. George had his first race at the age of eighteen at the Putney Velodrome in the 1890's and he continued to run for the next sixty years. Latterly he had contented himself with his second love - swimming and diving; and death came to him on the 4th of October when, after swimming three lengths at the Baths, he collapsed and died at the age of 82 years. In his heyday George was a member of the Highgate Harriers teams which dominated the Southern Cross Country Championships for a decade, and he was a member of their winning "National" teams in 1904 and 1905. He was a more than useful performer at any distance from 880 yards up to the Marathon, and was honoured by an invitation to compete at the Olympic Games, but this he had to decline for domestic reasons. We shall remember George Still with affection as a great character and sportsman and as a link with our early days when there were cross country courses to be found in the Battersea neighbourhood. items.s: To George Still of the Belgrave Harriers Farewell poem to George Still by L. Fabre, a 70-year-old Belgrave runner. I taught you how to swim, you taught me how to run, What a clean life it was, for it was full of fun, You started before me George and you never did pause, But watch for me Georgie for I am very close, And again full of fun, We may meet for that final great run, Farewell George, you were a great sport and I respected you. items.sum: Report of the Poly. Harriers road relay, where Dave Baulch set a club best and the Belgrave A team was 5th.
items.s: POLY. HARRIERS ROAD RELAY (8 x 3 miles) SEPT. 20TH. Report of the Poly. Harriers road relay, where Dave Baulch set a club best and the Belgrave A team was 5th. Conditions were perfect and personal bests cut by 30 sec. were the order of the day. On the first leg Dave Baulch ran 13.42 to set up a new Club best, only to be 250 yds. behind the leader, Roath(Walton), who sliced 16s. off the course record with a magnificent 13.01. A notable feature of the 'A' team was the fine running of R. Bhatia, who should be a great asset on the Brighton road. The 'A' team finished 5th. The 'B' team were 9th (second 'B'team), and at half-way they were still ahead of the strong Herne Hill 'A' team. Ken Miller, despite little training, looked very fit showing 14.08 - fastest of the 'B' team. The 'C' team finished 25th of the 31 starting teams. items.label: No. 137
items.h: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RELAY (SOUTHERN CLUBS) OCT.11TH
items.sum: Stage-by-stage account by Eric Hall of Belgrave's sixth place in the London to Brighton road relay for southern clubs, with a call to rebuild the club's running and the stage times.
items.s: LONDON TO BRIGHTON RELAY (SOUTHERN CLUBS) OCT.11TH Stage-by-stage account by Eric Hall of Belgrave's sixth place in the London to Brighton road relay for southern clubs, with a call to rebuild the club's running and the stage times. The Brighton, I am informed, is almost always held in fine weather, and this year was no exception. October 11th. was the sort of day when a trip to the sea is just what Doctor Brighton would order. As I am a newcomer to this business of road-relays, I needed quite a lot of persuading to enter into the spirit of things. After much coaxing I was waiting at Big Ben for the first stroke of ten to set 20 lightly clad figures on their way. At last Big Ben warmed up and the chime rang out clearly and they were off. (Thought - what happens if there is a false start? Perhaps they go home and wait till next year). That was that, I thought, as they disappeared out of sight but my chauffeur was already revving his car after a Le Mans type start, so I joined in the chase. Down Millbank and across Battersea Bridge where Brian Hallowell was nicely placed in ninth place after a leisurely start. Then satisfied that Brian knew what he was doing, we sped on to Clapham Common for the first change-over. Brian had moved up to seventh and away went Charlie Walker. Portsmouth had a slight lead from Brighton and T.V.H. Charlie did well in the early part, but was being closely followed. However, on arrival at Mitcham he had moved up to sixth. We had dropped further behind the leaders and the gaps had begun to appear. Lewis(Woodford) and Pape (Portsmouth) were in contrast here and it was surprising to see Pape go away quite easily. Dave Baulch, usually on a later stage, was having a change of scenery this year but as he was surrounded by Internationals he not surprisingly had to relinquish two vital places. At Purley it was Clive Shippen's turn to take his medicine and at nineteen miles we took a rough time check; Portsmouth led Woodford by thirty seconds with Herne Hill moving up well seventeen seconds behind. Then came a long gap until T.V.H. and Walton followed by Aylesford and Essex Beagles with Clive chasing hard. We were now four minutes behind Portsmouth - not a very bright outlook. When we eventually caught up with the runners again, (those motor driven coaches are a greater nuisance than the athletic type) we found Jim Masters in command. The manner in which he tackled the long climb through Redhill was ajoy to watch, he made short work of two of the intruders and we were back to sixth again. John Davies had the shortest trip of the day (hardly worth the bother of changing John!) and at Salfords Woodford had taken over from Pompey, we had improved slightly and were now three minutes and twenty seconds in arrears; it was felt that this was still too large a gap. The next man to show his paces was newcomer to the Brighton road, Mal Robinson. He had what I consider to be a very unpleasant stretch past Gatwick Airport; he held on to our position but unfortunately the gaps grew wider. Our next glimpse of the race was after Crawley, and Portsmouth were back in the lead. Pat Newell was doing the first of the two long legs for us and he was being closely followed by Ilford, Polytechnic and Hampstead in a bunch which looked rather ominous. However, Pat didn't let us down and we held our position. Just outside Bolney we had a grand view of the race and Pompey led by over a minute from Woodford. Eric Gebbett was doing his utmost to hold on to our place but the fifth team, T.V.H., were over three minutes in front. Harry Hicks was on this leg for Hampstead and looked very dangerous but Eric refused to be panicked and towards the end was moving away slightly. For us the race was now over, as the gaps were such that we required at least three top class three-milers; we could only hope that our remaining runners would hold our position. Charlie Dabbs had other ideas and put up the third fastest time for the tenth stage. He was relieved on the tricky Dale Hill stage by "veteran" Archie Bedford who put us well clear of the rest of the field. The last man, but by no means the least, was John Moore. Not for him a dramatic finish as for some previous Belgravians, nor the feeling of truimph, just the steady plod home unheralded save by the faithful supporters who had cheered their club-mates all the way from Mitcham. Our sixth position entitles us to compete in the National next April, but as we finished six minutes and forty-two seconds in arrears I do not hold out much hope for a Belgrave victory. This year's race was not particularly fast and we lost an average of eight seconds every mile. The supporters as always did a magnificent job of work, but only those with long years of service can remember a Belgrave win. Surely its about time they had another? I am not a very senior member, but when I became a Belgravian in 1948 we were National Cross Country Champions. We had many fine runners and as now a great tradition. Of recent years we have slipped rapidly down hill, but every club has its ups and downs, so what about an all-round effort; some serious training, then and only then will the results follow. Our walkers have proved that it can be done. Only a few years ago we weren't figuring in the results, so Jack Goswell thought it was about time we got back to our rightful position. Someone could do the same for the runners. All it requires is a large back and the ability not to take no for an answer. We have enough men capable of handling this job of welding the lads into a TEAM and thereby getting the results that the "old timers" achieved. This is not a new recipe, it is one which brought Belgrave fame in the past and will do the same again we hope in the near future. Eric Hall. Stage times with stage rankings in brackets:- 1 B. items.sum: Report of the five-club cross-country match at Dartford, where Belgrave won both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches.
items.s: MATCH AT DARTFORD - 18TH OCT. Report of the five-club cross-country match at Dartford, where Belgrave won both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches. This five-sided fixture involving Dartford H., City of Rochester A.C., Maidstone A.C., Kent A.C. and, of course, ourselves was the first event of the cross-country season, and following so closely on the London to Brighton relay was expected to be something of an anti-climax. Also, with our forces split between the Walton "10" and the organisation of our own open Youths road relay, a strong turn-out was not envisaged for such a distant fixture. However, all predictions were proved wrong with a splendid turn-out of seventeen, but which included only three of the previous week's twelve Brighton men. Once again we illustrated our great depth by winning both the five-a-side and eight-a-side matches. Owing to the uneven apportionment of Juniors in the five clubs it was decided to run both grades in one senior scoring race over 5½ miles. Despite the brisk start up a half-mile incline, John Moore wasn't satisfied with the pace and, accompanied by Bob Glover and J. Lyne of S.L.H.(2nd claim Kent A.C.), forged ahead to establish a clear lead of thirty yards after 1¼ miles. Shortly afterwards he had the misfortune to go off course at a point which should clearly have had a marksman rather than a flag. By the time he had been called back and rejoined the race he had dropped to 25th place. It says much for his determination and ever improving form that he was able to fight his way back to fourth place at the finish. Approaching the end of the first lap Miller, Thompson, Glover, Bedford and Shippen were in close attendance around tenth position with John Moore moving through fast after his mishap. Morrison of Dartford and Ellam of Rochester were sharing a lead of 75 yds. Ellam eventually pulled away to win by eighteen seconds in a new course record time of 26.12. Shippen moved through well over the last mile and he was closely followed by Archie Bedford who had run steadily throughout. Bob Glover found out too late that one mustn't underestimate the finishing speed of those behind, especially when they include an accomplished half miler like Gerald Batty of Rochester! With Miller, Thompson and Bob Taylor backing up very closely Belgrave were assured of the team race. One of our recent recruits, John Collier, ran well in his first race for the Club and should soon become a more than useful runner. If the remainder of the winter fixtures are supported as well as this one, then Belgrave is indeed on the road back to their all-conquering past in cross-country running. Result:- 4,J. items.s: HIGHGATE OPEN 7 MILES WALK 25TH OCT. Report and result of the Highgate open 7 miles walk, where Stan Vickers was second to record-breaker Ken Matthews and Belgrave won the scratch and handicap team races. The first open race of the season must inevitably cause some anxiety as to how our teams have weathered and how they are likely to fare in subsequent championships. This worry was soon dispelled however, as our team, led by Stan Vickers, quickly established themselves amongst the leaders. A great race for individual honours took place between Ken Matthews of Royal Sutton Coldfield and Stan, with the former just getting the verdict in a time which shattered the previous course record by more than two minutes. The remainder of our team walked extremely well and with Ray Hall, Ray Middleton, George Checkley and John Knifton we easily won the scratch team race. We also won the team handicap, which is an important feature of these open walks, with Stan, R. Hall, R. Middleton and J. Knifton. It was an added pleasure to note the good walking of our younger men, particularly that of Brian Cornick and Robert Barns. 1st Belgrave H. 45 pts. 2nd Highgate H. 57 pts. 3rd Woodford 62 pts. 2 S.F. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's eighth place in the Chelmsford road relay, their first visit since winning the trophy in 1952, with stage-by-stage account and times.
items.s: CHELMSFORD ROAD RELAY 25TH OCT. Report of Belgrave's eighth place in the Chelmsford road relay, their first visit since winning the trophy in 1952, with stage-by-stage account and times. This was our first visit to Chelmsford since 1952 when we won the magnificent trophy for the second successive year. Unfortunately, the date now clashes with our five-mile cross-country handicap, but surely six of our best men can be spared each year to at least "show face" at such an important event; and so it was. Our six were Bob Glover, Malcolm Robinson, Alan Black, Eric Gebbett, Charlie Walker and Dave Baulch; three relative newcomers to road relay racing and three "veterans". Fifty-six teams started and it was soon apparent that many clubs treat this race as their event of the year. It was good to see Bob Glover turning out for us in this type of event, and his running justified the confidence many have in him. After a mile he was still amongst the leaders and a little later began to force the pace on Lewis(Woodford), Stacey(T.V.H.) and Cornell(Chelmsford). However, he was unable to maintain this speed and finished in 12th position. Malcolm Robinson set off in great style for lap 2 and after about two miles had passed no less than seven men, being only ten seconds behind fourth place. He continued to narrow the gap before he in turn was caught and passed, after quite a battle, by Haith of T.V.H. Malcolm returned our fastest time of the day - 15.24. Young Alan Black, undeterred by the star names around him, ran a very sensible 3rd stage, dropping places only to Sando and O'Gorman, each of whom broke the course record. White took Woodford into a lead here which they kept to the end, while Bert Ingles drew away from Alan to increase the Valley's lead over us to 29s. Eric Gebbett took over in eighth position with three men in close attendance and promptly showed how well he runs in company by shaking off all three and gaining two further places into the bargain. All this over a distance which is little more than a sprint to Eric. J. Haslam, with a time only seven seconds faster than Eric's took T.V.H. into third place, five places ahead of the Bels who conceded a further place to Chelmsford. Charlie Walker set off on leg 5 and soon passed Chelmsford to regain sixth place but was eventually overtaken by Mayatt of Aylesford and Irons of Victoria Park. This was not the Charlie of old, although his time was faster than many recorded in 1952 when 15 minutes had yet to be beaten. However, when he handed over to Dave Baulch for the final leg we were still within 14 sec. of sixth place. Unfortunately Dave was nowhere near his inspired best and we had to be content with our eighth position. As a point of interest, our three experienced runners recorded an aggregate time of 46.45 while the inexperienced trio totalled 46.34! - the shape of things to come? Eric Hall was a further two minutes back in third place. By finishing four men in twelve places we easily won the team race and retained the Berman Cup. items.s: CLUB 7 MILES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP DEC.6TH Report and result of the club 7 miles cross-country championship, won by Charlie (Chas.) Walker from Pat Newell and John Moore. A bright but cold day brought forth a rather small field for a club of our size, but perhaps quality of individuals takes precedence over quantity of team runners these days. A notable non-starter was Dave Baulch, suffering from a heavy cold, who, despite the assertions of the old-timers that a race would do him good, wisely refrained from competing. A steady start meant a large bunch of runners in the lead for the first two miles, but as the weaker flesh fell away it was left to Chas. Walker, John Moore and Pat Newell to decide the issue, with Eric Gebbett, Malcolm Robinson and Alan Black forming the spearhead of the second bunch. At the top of the hockey field on the second lap Chas. sprinted ahead of Newell and opening up a gap ran home a fairly comfortable winner, with John Moore finishing a close third after a well judged race. items.sum: Light-hearted spectator's notes ('Random notes of an Idle Fellow') on the Cambridge H. 7 miles open walk at Eltham, won by Stan Vickers with Belgrave taking the team race, with results.
items.s: CAMBRIDGE H. 7 MILES OPEN WALK. DEC.6TH Light-hearted spectator's notes ('Random notes of an Idle Fellow') on the Cambridge H. 7 miles open walk at Eltham, won by Stan Vickers with Belgrave taking the team race, with results. Random notes of an Idle Fellow The cold and cheerless afternoon afforded an excellent excuse for turning up at Eltham and exclaiming "I am resting", as a reason for standing on the side-line and offering to all and sundry, "free of charge", words of encouragement, advice or derision, according to my fancy. It was a wonderful change from ploughing my usual weary way, to achieve, after much sweat, effort and banter, some unmentionable time. The only reward being the tussle with "so and so" and the grand comradeship of those who "walk the roads". What were my impressions of this band of brothers who wear the Claret and Gold with such distinction? If pride be the prerogative of bantam cocks, then I was a very proud bantam cock when battle was joined and our contingent, led by that superlative walker Stan Vickers, flay the enemy at every level Space is too limited to more than just refer to the tenacity and pugnaciousness of Eric Hall, the daintiness of George Williams which camoufleges no ordinary resoluteness, the strength of Ray Middleton who must be a future champion, the potential powers of Terry Clark and Brian Cornick, and so through the team to our last man, Percy Wilson, who so typifies the fun and enjoyment obtained from the sport. The ten prizes awarded to our men is a measure of their success and a study of the following results will clearly show how they dominated the proceedings. In conclusion, I would emphasize the amount of fun and enjoyment that can be obtained from watching these athletic competitions and ask you, when free, to support the current fixture, be it running or walking. It will be a great encouragement to the competitors concerned and the effort will be well repaid by the comradeship obtained from a greater knowledge of your fellow members. 1 S.F.
