items.sum: Club news column: Ken England is very ill with disseminated sclerosis, the Coleman brothers' late-night walking training is recalled, Len Herbert has lost the urge to race, and Jack Brown writes from troubled Cyprus.
items.s: Here and There Club news column: Ken England is very ill with disseminated sclerosis, the Coleman brothers' late-night walking training is recalled, Len Herbert has lost the urge to race, and Jack Brown writes from troubled Cyprus. Many members will remember Ken England, a rather tough determined cross-country runner of a few years back. Ginger Kennedy writes to tell us that Ken is a very ill man, now hardly able to walk due to disseminated schlerosis. We feel sure that all readers will join us in wishing him a speedy recovery. They used to breed 'em tough in the old days, and the brothers Joe and Len Coleman were no exception. None of your fancy 9 to 5 hours for them; in fact at well past midnight both could have been found still hard at work in their respective trades, printing and catering. But training had to be fitted in and as both were walkers this was carried out by a brisk walk home from work at about 2 a.m. Needless to say they would both walk back to work the next morning. Can anyone beat this? Len Herbert is apparently still running several times a week but says he has lost the urge to race. His brother Eric is now married to a Dutch girl and he has now fully recovered from his serious climbing accident. Jack Brown writes to say how really difficult life has become in Cyprus; the strain on everyone is intense and being practically confined to their house Jack and his wife Betty and son Malcolm find their greatest enjoyment is derived from their record player. We hope it won't be long before commonsense prevails, bringing a return to normal conditions in Cyprus and that before long Jack will be back to don his Claret and Gold vest again to good account. items.sum: Letter from Harry Shields, prompted by a 1934 training schedule for the Southern Counties and English cross-country championships, regretting that no member was selected for the Inter-Counties and urging members to focus training on the main championships.
items.s: SINGLENESS OF PURPOSE Letter from Harry Shields, prompted by a 1934 training schedule for the Southern Counties and English cross-country championships, regretting that no member was selected for the Inter-Counties and urging members to focus training on the main championships. Dear Fellow Members, I wonder how many of us, with the approach of "Spring Cleaning Season", suddenly become filled with a desire to have a clear out of our accumulated momentoes aquired over the ages? How many of us start, only to get bogged down in browsing over those relics of the past? Such was my fate when, a little prematurely perhaps, it was forced on me that, if domestic peace was to be maintained, then a major surgical operation was required on my heaped up store of minute books, nomination forms, programmes and all the other impedimenta gathered in club and association activities. Many papers recalling "life and death" contentions of previous years were ruthlessly destroyed, but I could not help dwelling on the three page "Schedule of training for Southern Counties and English Cross-Country Championships 1934" It commences," In the past the cross-country members of our Club have entered the New Year without any definite idea as regards training for any particular race other than running twice or three times a week as members of a pack or otherwise" Then follows a summary of improvement which should arise from systematic training. A list of eleven exercises is tabulated, to be carried out every morning. These include dumbell exercises and hints on general hygiene and diet. The week by week training schedule is graduated until immediately previous to the Southern Championships; it reads:- Monday - 3 miles in 18 mins. Tuesday - 7 " " 37 " Wednesday - 3 " " 18 " Thursday - 3 " " 18 " Friday - Complete rest except for exercises. Saturday - 12 miles in 65 mins. Sunday - Stroll about 20 miles In addition, every morning, a stroll part way to work is recommended. Even in the light of modern experience it is an extraordinarily far-sighted document and of its benefits the performances of those who were influenced by it are perhaps the best yardstick. You will perhaps excuse my nostalgic reviews of the past, but at Parliament Hill recently on the occasion of the Inter-Counties Championship there was not one single member selected to represent his County. It appeared particularly incredible when I thought of the ability of many of our athletes only to remember how quickly they break off at a tangent for some "out of season event". Such actions seem almost escapist from the realities of the principle targets. This inevitably leads to the question, " what are the targets?" The answer to this must be, "The Championships sponsored by the governing bodies at the particular time of the year". These Championships must be given prime consideration if the maximum benefit is to be obtained from our great sport. I appreciate that taking lessons from the past is open to criticism but the conclusion is inescapeable that singleness of purpose is absolutely essential if the greatest success as an individual or as a club is to be achieved. Is it not worthwhile to discuss your training ideas with your section leader with a view to formulating a schedule for modern needs? For my part the influence of these early schedules on a very varied athletic career has been considerable. In conclusion, the best of luck and although the way to success may be difficult and weary, do not be diverted by the glitter of side-shows and above all ensure that there is thought and direction in all that you do. Sincerely yours. Harry Shields Harry Shields Harry Shields Southern Cross Country Championships English Cross-Country Championships Inter-Counties Parliament Hill

items.s: FIELD EVENTS GOSSIP Field events column by Field Events Secretary T.C. Jones: Belgrave men in the 1958 British ranking lists, hopes for the Sward Trophy, and the club's pre-season Open Meeting at Battersea on March 14th. In welcoming another New Year we look forward to the coming summer season with hopes of greater successes. Our performances last year were not, on the whole, as good as in some previous years but nevertheless it is good to see some of our men's names appearing in the British ranking list with the following marks:- Also appearing in the lists was Dick Harris, an ex-Belgravian now in New Zealand, with a 47'4½" Shot Putt and 146'9" in the Discus. Whilst mentioning Shot Putters we are pleased to welcome Derek McCorquindale who recorded a best of 50'3" and was in the English team at Cardiff. Young John Roche who is just over 15 must not be forgotten as his 5'7" in the High Jump was easily a best Club performance for a Belgravian of his age. His progress over the next few years will be watched with great interest, as also will that of John Sams who won both Southern and A.A.A. Junior 200 yards Hurdles Championships. With our best performers of last year, Derek McCorquindale and perhaps one of our reasonable Javelin throwers getting nearer the 200' mark we should put up a really good show in"The Sward", Trophy, especially as John Sams will then be a Senior and Charlie Jones will be out to make the grade at 440 yards hurdling. John Powell Jones who won the Welsh Shot Championship two seasons ago must not be left out of the reckoning as I hear that he has recovered from his back injury. Some winter and early season training should be got in with our sights on "The Sward" and pre-season competition will be provided by the T.V.H. meeting in February and our own Open Meeting on March 14th. The latter is at Battersea and the events are as follows:- Shot Discus Javelin Pole Vault High Jump Long Jump Triple Jump There are no prizes and no entry fees, but your entries are expected in full support of this Club venture. We have welcome news of Ted Gaworski in that he is back at work and progressing. He promises that he will be back on the Field at the earliest moment. T.C. items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Eric Hall's humorous account of the trip to the Great Britain versus France match in Paris, where Stan Vickers won the 10,000 metres walk with Hall second.
items.s: GAY PAREE Eric Hall's humorous account of the trip to the Great Britain versus France match in Paris, where Stan Vickers won the 10,000 metres walk with Hall second. A 10,000 metres walk was included in the Great Britain versus France match in Paris on the 13/14th. Sept. Stan Vickers and myself were lucky enough to get the trip. Behind that bald statement lies a wealth of incident which could fill this magazine for the next few issues. We arrived in Paris late Friday evening and found our quarters in the National Institute des Sports at Vincennes, some six miles from the centre of Paris. No doubt this was specially selected by the B.A.A.B. The quarters themselves were comfortable but the meals were of microscopic proportions. After what was by even continental standards, a very meagre breakfast a few of us adjourned to the nearest market to stock up for the rest of the stay. Stan was appointed C.[illegible]. stores and the rest of us supplied the money and the lingo. After a short lesson on French Stan was pushed into a shop and asked to buy some honey. In less time than it takes Peter Radford to run 100 metres he was back, protesting,"I can't understand a word she's saying". Apparently the poor girl didn't speak Hindustani! Stan's next attempt was very much better, he wanted some grapefruit, so after yelling it in French for some moments he was 'bout to give up when the girl turned on a dazzling smile and said, in perfect English,"Ah, you would like some grapefruit". That was the last we heard of Stan's French! Saturday afternoon was very warm, so after taking part in the march-past we decided to "do" the town. Only 5000 people were at the stadium so we didn't want to be conspicuous. Somehow or other we made our way to the Arc de Triomphe and there we made an error of judgement when someone suggested crossing the road, the person concerned being a sprinter- naturally! After a couple of attempts and some"lifting" by Stan and myself we made it. Stan was most disappointed as nearly everyone was American so he couldn't practise his French. The stadium was some 12 miles from our quarters so we were quite pleased with ourselves when we got safely back. This is a feat which Jack Goswell couldn't do in London, let alone Paris. Sunday was one of the hottest days of the year and in the morning we basked in the sun (that all too rare thing this summer). Stan and I duly performed in the afternoon and of course our European Gold-Medallist romped home in 47m.3s. with myself second, after some very anxious moments, in 48m.44s. Attane of France was third in 48m.57s. Not world shattering times but just good enough. Once again we forgot about the match in which, incidently, the walk did not count, and moved smartly to the Buffet- Bar to quench a hard earned thirst. On our return to the stands we found that while we had been emptying bottles, Stan Eldon had been doing the same to the steeplechase pit, much to the amusement of the 5000 staunch supporters who had turned up for the second day. The match itself produced some very fine running, but it was a very one-sided affair, with England winning all the track events and finishing up with nearly twice as many points as the French. As L'Equipe pointed out the next day, our overall supremacy was equalled by our victory in the final event, the 4 x 400 metres relay, which we won by eight seconds. As soon as the meeting was over we dashed back for a meal and were then taken to the Folies Bergere. I will not attempt to describe the various acts but leave it to what I feel sure are very adequate imaginations! We left the show at midnight and made for the Institute via several cafes and didn't finally arrive back until around 3 a.m. - much too late for bed! Much could still be written of Stan's adventures - his near arrest at the Folies, his missing the way home after volunteering to act as guide to three female members of the team - it only took him two hours to do two miles that night! It wouldn't really be fair to blacken his character any more. He probably had the last laugh on me next morning. Before we left London someone had most unkindly told Stan that it was my birthday on the Monday. Stan remembered this at the most inopportune moment and so at Le Bourget a full choir of British athletes sang "Happy Birthday", it was much worse than the Boeing 707 warming up outside! items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Plea to value the club's older, less active members, whose subscriptions and gifts fund its 43 championship trophies and its expenses.
items.s: A QUESTION OF AGE Plea to value the club's older, less active members, whose subscriptions and gifts fund its 43 championship trophies and its expenses. Having heard a number of comments recently regarding our older and less active members, with suggestions that we might be better off without some of them, leads me to wonder if these critics realise how much the Club owes to these enthusiastic supporters who, year after year, and without any hope of personal gain, continue to subscribe regularly to help provide facilities for the younger members, which, without such support would not be available. A study of the Club Handbook will show that we have 43 Championship trophies, valued, according to the Balance, at £1200. These have, in the main, been provided by or in association with, some of the "old" members to encourage competition among the younger ones. The financing of these Championships on track, field and road and also over the country, is only one of the many large items of expenditure which need the support of far more than the hundred or so active athletes who take part in them. Since Amateur Athletics remains one of the few things which are not State aided let us be grateful to those who, because of their affection for the name of Belgrave and in return for the pleasure they have gained in the past, continue to give their support wholeheartedly, generously and in a spirit of comradeship. A "Not so old 'un"

items.label: No. 137
items.sum: Light-hearted note on the 1958 Annual General Meeting, praising President Frank Webb.
items.s: A.G.M. 1958 Light-hearted note on the 1958 Annual General Meeting, praising President Frank Webb. A motley crowd turned up, including most of the "old faithfuls". The meeting always begins with orations from the chair with varying degrees of linguistic ability, but who cares! The old cry, "no change", heralds the appointment of the Officers who must have lots of time to spare, (wait for it) good show chaps! Our old friend Frank tried to create a diversion but was really shot down in flames by Bomber Lucas. The mystery of the missing vests could have caused acute distress to one of our members, but who said that the age of chivalry is dead and so, with age old charm, an apology was offered and dignity restored. Frank Webb is a worthy President, unassuming, no sting in his tongue. A.W.P. Bomber Lucas Bomber Lucas Frank Webb Frank Webb President A.W.P. A.W.P. A.G.M.

items.label: No. 137
items.h: A FEW WORDS FROM YOUR SOCIAL SECRETARY
items.sum: Social Secretary Bert Jordon's notes: poorly supported dances, thanks for the children's party of 11 January 1959, a coming Social and Dance, coaches for the London to Brighton relay, and a proposed summer outing.
items.s: A FEW WORDS FROM YOUR SOCIAL SECRETARY Social Secretary Bert Jordon's notes: poorly supported dances, thanks for the children's party of 11 January 1959, a coming Social and Dance, coaches for the London to Brighton relay, and a proposed summer outing. The Socials and Dances held so far this season have not been very well supported. I would like to see many more members taking advantage of these functions. We have a good class Band and those who do support us on these occasions have a very enjoyable time. Why not come along and see for yourself at the next Social, I am sure you will want to come again. Children's Party - Jan.11th, 1959 This function was a great success, the children enjoyed the entertainer "Uncle Jim" very much. He held their attention for a whole hour with his feats of magic and he ended with a Punch and Judy show, which the Mums and Dads enjoyed just as much as the children. I would like to take this opportunity of thanking, firstly the Ladies, Mrs Carter, Mrs Shepherd, Mrs Savage and Mrs Jordon for all their hard work, both on Saturday afternoon and Sunday, in preparing and serving the children's tea and serving refreshments for the parents, and also Mrs Lucas for her help with the children's tea and entertainments. Also Dick Savage for his efforts as Father Christmas, which he performed excellently, and for his help in the kitchen, also Bill Lucas and Bob Taylor for their hard work in entertaining the children, and Malcolm Robinson for his assistance in the kitchen, and Tom Carter for his general assistance during the afternoon, and all the people, too numerous to mention, who helped to make the party a success. There must have been many more children who could have been present but whose names were not given to me. So I would like to mention that children from twelve months to twelve years old are welcome to attend this annual party. There surely could be many more than the thirty-six who attended this year's For your future entertainment A Social and Dance will be held on Saturday 24th March. This will be the last of the season and I am hoping that you will all give it your support. London to Brighton Relay Two coaches have been booked for spectators to follow the National Relay on the 11th April. Tickets will, as usual, be 10/- each and they can be obtained from Bob Taylor. An early application will be appreciated, as it will enable us to book a further coach if necessary. Come along and cheer our team to Brighton. Summer Outing It is hoped to arrange an outing to a seaside resort on a Sunday in June or July. Would members please let me have their views on this proposal. Thanking you for your support during the season and looking forward to even greater support in the future. Bert Jordon. items.sum: Editorial thanking contributors, welcoming shot putter Don McCorquindale, noting early-season form, praising "our Sten"'s win in Berlin and hinting the editors would like to hand over the gazette.
items.s: EDITORIAL Editorial thanking contributors, welcoming shot putter Don McCorquindale, noting early-season form, praising "our Sten"'s win in Berlin and hinting the editors would like to hand over the gazette. Dear Fellow Members, It never rains but what it pours and before going to press we have been inundated with contributions for the magazine from all quarters. So please, those critics whose voices are exercised more frequently than their pens, don't itemise what has been omitted but be thankful that a far greater number of articles have been submitted. Once again we have a fine weight putter in the Club, Don McCorquindale, who has made a fine start to the 1959 season. Charlie Jones must be greatly pleased with such an acquisition for our field events section. Brian Morris and John Davies have already recorded good times for the 440 yds. and 1500 metres respectively, whilst Alan Black and Malcolm Robinson look set for their best seasons yet. We are all justly proud of "our Sten" for his great win in Berlin. This was really one out of the bag and his margin over Matthews was quite astounding. Lastly, a note of warning and possibly of hope. We have edited the Belgravian now for almost three years and as active marathon runners we feel that we have made our contribution towards the revival of the magazine and that perhaps some other aspiring editors in the Club would like to try their hand. When the A.G.M. comes round again we hope to be able to hand over this gazette to a new editor. For approximately £43 you can travel by steamer and rail, via Newhaven, Dieppe, Paris and Modane to Rome, be accommodated in a good hotel where you will breakfast and have an evening meal and see the athletic events in the stadium on an all-day ticket! During the Games there will be two free days when you can partake in any of the many sight-seeing tours. items.s: "HORWOOD" CUP CHAMPIONSHIP - DEC.13TH. Report and results of the Horwood Cup walking championship, won again by Ray Middleton from John Knifton and newcomer K. Jones. Ray Middleton repeated his victory of last year. Oscar Horwood, a great Club man, would have been delighted to see another very good winner on the list of fine walkers whose names are recorded on his cup. Ray has the potential of a champion just as surely as we saw it in others who have fulfilled that promise. He led in excellent style throughout. John Knifton, a few years younger than Ray, was placed for the third year in succession, which shows that hard discipline of training for several years is necessary to win this event. A newcomer, K. Jones, did very well to finish third. Bob Barnes continues to improve and was unlucky to lose third place to this tough opponent. The rest of the race was keenly fought, as always, and many unplaced were working as hard as those who gained the medals. It was good to see Joe Wilson going so well after his accident and Bert East must have taken part in about twenty-five "Horwood Cup" races since the cup was instituted. At the same time there were novices who will be tomorrow's victors if they persevere. Harry Evans, an old friend of Oscar's, was there to see fair play and to give advice where needed. The ceremony of prize-giving brings a satisfying conclusion to an afternoon's sport and we were reminded of the thanks we owe to those who regularly organise the provision of prizes when, for once, the prizes and medals had, unfortunately, not arrived Handicap result:- 1 M. items.s: MATCH v. BLACKHEATH & H.H.H. AT HAYES - JAN.10TH. Report of the 7½ mile cross-country match against Blackheath and Herne Hill at Hayes, won by Blackheath; John Moore was second behind Mike Maynard and Chris Thompson retired injured. Despite the Mitcham '15' accounting for many of our members we were still able to produce fifteen runners for this fixture, as against sixteen by Blackheath and nine by Herne Hill. The 7½ mile course had been extremely muddy the previous week but had since frozen hard. As a result the going was particularly hazardous, and three runners retired with twisted ankles on the "plough" while many put caution before performance. Mike Maynard set a fast pace at the start and was comfortably leading after a mile from John Moore and Chris Thompson with Clive Shippen and the Blackheath captain, A.W. Wood, a further 50 yards down. After 4½ miles John Moore had established himself in second place, about 200 yards behind Maynard, while Wood and Shippen, still running together, had virtually caught Thompson. At this stage Chris badly twisted his ankle in one of the frozen furrows and although he tried gamely to continue he was forced to retire. However, he had done sufficient to show once more what tremendous potential he possesses, and Junior honours could no doubt come his way during the next two seasons. Meanwhile John Davies and Jim Heathfield were doing battle with a string of Blackheath men a little further back. Both of our boys lost ground on the dangerous stretches with a sensible "safety first" policy but made it up in the last mile or so of even going; John, in particular, gaining several places. Maynard won convincingly by about 450 yards from Moore who ran exceedingly well and was always moving away from the Blackheath man in third place. Thompson's mishap did not affect the match result which was won by Blackheath's superior packing. Results:- 2, J. Moore 46.18; 4, C. Shippen 47.46; 8, J. Davies 48.37; 14, J. Heathfield 49.48; 19, J. items.sum: Report of the R.A.F. seven miles walking championship at Harpur Hill, led throughout by Terry Clark.
items.s: R.A.F. SEVEN MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the R.A.F. seven miles walking championship at Harpur Hill, led throughout by Terry Clark. This year's R.A.F. race might be described as one of Belgrave's triumphs. It was held at Harpur Hill, in North Derbyshire, on 28th January; a day when the bright sunshine and clean, crisp air made racing pleasant in spite of the hilly terrain. The course consisted of one small lap and a larger one of fairly good roads with not too much traffic. Terry Clark headed the field from the start and was never overtaken. The good walking of a "dark horse" in the person of Flt.Lt. O.G.J. Hotston during the early stages of the race gave rise to surprise and a measure of anxiety. Usually a cross-country runner for R.A.F. Lindholme, this Officer went after Terry and tenaciously hung on to second place until he began to tire. A.C. Desmond of R.A.F. Bridgenorth and Essex Beagles came through after the first three quarters of a mile in an endevour to get on terms with Terry and, in the meantime, Bernard Eglinton was battling it out for fourth place with Nigel Deeks of R.A.F. Cosford and Met. Walking Club. The former subsequently gained a lead of about thirty five yards. At two and a half miles, Holston was slowing down perceptibly and the second Belgrave man succeeded in passing him at about three miles. The course was now a steady climb to the five-mile point, followed by a steep downhill gradient and an equally severe uphill grind of about a mile to the finish. Terry quickened his pace and disappeared from view but Desmond seemed to slow a little on the hills. Deeks made a valiant bid for third place in the last mile and a half, actually drawing almost level with Eglinton on the last hill. On this occasion, however, age prevailed by a mere ten seconds. 1 Cpl. T.B. Clark 57m. 13s. Belgrave 2 A.C. M. Desmond 59m. 55s. Essex Beagles 3 F/S. B. Eglinton 60m. 32s. Belgrave 4 Sgt. N. items.sum: Report of the Southern Counties cross-country championships hosted by Aylesford Paper Mills: Belgrave youths fielded only three, the seniors were fifth team behind Thames Valley Harriers and the juniors seventh behind Shaftesbury Harriers, with Belgrave results.
items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS - FEB.14TH. Report of the Southern Counties cross-country championships hosted by Aylesford Paper Mills: Belgrave youths fielded only three, the seniors were fifth team behind Thames Valley Harriers and the juniors seventh behind Shaftesbury Harriers, with Belgrave results. Hosts for this year's event were Aylesford Paper Mills who, not for the first time, provided ideal facilities for championships of this nature. The course was ideal for runners and spectators alike, while the weather man had assisted the arrangements by providing perfect conditions underfoot and a fine sunny day into the bargain. YOUTHS EVENT (3 miles) Belgrave's day did not get off to a very good start, for with four to score in the team event we were only able to field three runners - Eric Penny, Mike Smithers and Roy Bagley. How many of our absent youths appreciated just how much their presence was needed? Eric, in 114th position, led our trio home; all of whom performed creditably. No doubt the efforts of these lads will be better rewarded when some of Tom Carter's promising youngsters move into their ranks. The event was won by Dave Harvey (Mitcham) who ran an excellently judged race to beat Smith(Deptford Park). It is interesting to note that Harvey is second string in his club to Harris, a 'flu victim during this event, and also that all these Mitcham youths are enthusiastically coached by the ex-Belgrave Mitchell brothers. We congratulate them on their excellent results. SENIOR EVENT (9 miles) Influenza had taken its toll of many leading athletes, but this made the team race more open than ever. Unfortunately, for a variety of reasons, Archie Bedford, John Davies, Colin Collis and Clive Shippen were unable to run, so with six to score and a "12 cup" in the offing we were able to start nine only. The number was eight to begin with but Malcolm Robinson, despite a suspect ankle, made a fine gesture in offering to run, thus making our entry look more respectable. Yet again the Arthur Whitehead "dustbin" sent the field on its way and after a ½ mile Pat Newell was 14th with Chanin(S.L.H.) leading from Ibbottson and Norris. John Moore had also got off to a good start, being in the forties, with Malcolm next man in the eighties. Charlie Walker, Eric Gebbett and Dave Baulch were labouring around the hundred mark. At two miles, with Maynard(H.H.H.) leading from Eldon and Knight, Pat was 15th, John 46th and our sixth scoring man in the nineties. At six miles, Eldon had established a substantial lead from Knight and Sando with Maynard 4th. Our lads had shewn considerable improvement in their team placings and were steadily pulling back the opposition with six men now in 87 and eight in 126. In the last mile the whole team made an extra special effort, pulling back over forty places amongst them. Special mention must go to our first and last man; to Pat Newell on his excellent 14th place and Alan Bishop for his most creditable 151st on this very fast course. Belgrave were the first team to finish seven, and also eight, runners but Old Belgravians will no doubt wince to hear that no club qualified for the twelve cup. Ex-members, Geoff Goode and Steve Charlton were seen running for their new clubs. Semi-retired Bagnall would have been our third scoring man with his 56th place!! Over 400 finished. 37 teams closed in. JUNIOR EVENT (6 miles) Apart from the unfortunate absence of Chris Thompson through injury, the Juniors were at full strength and following his excellent running the previous week hopes were pinned on a forward position by Alan Black. These hopes appeared to be well founded when, after a ½ mile, Alan was seen to be in third place, well backed up by Ken Miller and John Thresher in the early twenties and Trevor Hart in the sixties. A little after this, however, he had dropped back to join Ken and John and soon after dropped out altogether with severe stomach cramp; a nasty blow to both Alan and the team. After 2½ miles Howard(Watford) led the field from Lindsell (Portsmouth) and Baker(Walton). Ken Miller was now 29th, John Thresher 50th, Derek Crookes 92nd and Jim Radford 107th; Trevor Hart being forced to drop back a considerable way with trouble from a shoulder ailment. Derek and Jim moved through very strongly on the last lap to reach the sixties and nineties respectively. Boquets go to Ken Miller for his fine return to form after his recent chest trouble and to Trevor Hart for pluckily finishing the course. Despite being without their two best runners the team still managed to finish 7th out of the thirty teams to close in. Approx. 250 finished. 30 teams closed in. An excellent meal was provided by our hosts after the Championships, and the prizes were presented by their General Manager F.W. Amies Esq. Arthur Whitehead produced his most valuable result sheets again for distribution, and as usual they disappeared like gold dust; a fitting end to a day of keenly contested and exciting competition. items.s: COUNTY 10 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIPS. FEB.28TH Report of the county 10 miles walk championships: Belgrave's 'A' team won the Surrey title at Kingston led by Eric Hall, while a depleted team (as Cadogan A.C.) was fifth in Middlesex at Regents Park. SURREY - at Kingston Although the 'flu bug was still affecting our walkers, and overnight we had word that Ray Middleton had succumbed, it was with good heart that our two teams faced the starter. Our 'A' team won in devastating fashion with 17 points to Surrey A.C's. 33. The 'B' team, which was expected to be placed, was seriously weakened by re-arrangement to overcome the losses due to sickness and finished fourth. Comments on individuals must be headed by the continued great walking of Eric Hall who finished first. He was ably supported by George Williams 2nd, Ray Hall 6th and Terry Clark(still a junior) 8th. The fine walking of John Knifton in his first 10 mile race was encouraging. MIDDLESEX at Regents Park A very depleted team lined up for the start, and for the first time for many years we were unplaced. Ken Jones, who has the makings of a fine walker (he is an ex-runner) incurred the Judge's displeasure at an early stage and this further weakened our chances. How upsetting these decisions are, yet how important good judging is to the welfare of the sport. Do not be deterred Ken but take the opportunity to profit by your experience. items.s: NATIONAL C.C. CHAMPIONSHIPS AT PETERBOROUGH. MARCH 7TH. Report of the National cross-country championships at Peterborough, lamenting falling support and Belgrave's record-worst senior score of 980 points, with Belgrave senior, junior and youth positions (Ken Miller is given as 49th in the text but 66 in the positions list). The National was, at one time, the event of the year for Belgrave, and both competitors and supporters talked of nothing else for weeks before. In this modern age, however, the race passes almost unnoticed - the runners treat it as a pennance and the supporters are practically non-existant. How can we expect to regain the championship with such an attitude. Our runners must approach this race with the will to win and not with the idea that providing they turn out they have done their duty. The non-active members of the Club, and those athletes not chosen to compete, must turn up in force to encourage, cajole, drive, plead and use every means in their power to ensure our teams meet with success. Nothing helps a runner more than to have adequate support and to know that the Club as a whole is behind him, willing him to give of his best. Special trains and coaches are almost invariably arranged at low costs to transport supporters to the race so there is no excuse for missing events of such importance. There is much satisfaction to be gained from seeing your club mates racing in big championships and opportunity is also provided to see the "stars" in action. When a club is going through a bad patch, such as Belgrave is at present, the need for keen support is greater than ever, so if you want to see the "Bels" back to their past glories show an interest in their training, racing in Club events and particularly in major championships. The least said about this year's race the better. We were never in the hunt and our final score of 980 points is an all time record, never, we hope, to be repeated. Even Pat Newell who was our main hope could not get going and finished in the most disappointing position of 59th. The remainder appeared to have no life whatsoever and were certainly not in the same form as at the Southern a few weeks earlier. Individual positions:- 59, P. Newell; 136, C. Shippen; 158, D. Baulch; 174, E. Gebbett; 205, A. Bedford; 248, C. Walker; 266, L.C. Bishop; 335, E. Short; 347, J. Heathfield. The Juniors fared little better than the Seniors and as the runners passed us soon after the start we wondered whether any of our boys were there. Only Ken Miller, in 49th place, was in the first hundred. Alan Black, our best junior, was well down the field and only started to run over the last mile or two, when he made about seventy places. items.s: SOUTHERN COUNTIES 7 MILE TRACK WALK. MARCH 7TH. Report of the Southern Counties 7 mile track walk and supporting 6 mile races, with "Our Stan" absent through 'flu and a judging decision against George Williams, plus Belgrave placings. The main event was preceded by a Junior 6 miles in which John Knifton walked well to finish 4th. He was ably supported, a little way back, by Brian Gibbs. Another supporting event for 6 miles in the hour badges was then held and it was very pleasing to see Fred Denny finish second. It was a great pity that in the main event the holder, "Our Stan" was unable to take part as he was still laid low with 'flu. I am sure all will agree that his presence adds lustre and interest to any meeting. We still had five representatives in the field of forty and although major honours did not come our way a good reckoning was given. From our point of view this meeting was marred by an unpredictable judging decision given against George Williams when he was laying a comfortable second. George's heart is big enough to overcome this set-back but these unfathomable judgments are disturbing. 13 R.C. Hall 57.55 21 B. Eglinton 61.58 26 J. Morris 64.01 27 J. items.sum: Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford road relay, where Belgrave finished second to Woodford Green A.C., who set a course record.
items.s: ILFORD ROAD RELAY. MARCH 14TH Stage-by-stage report of the Ilford road relay, where Belgrave finished second to Woodford Green A.C., who set a course record. This has always been a popular event with our boys and acts as a relief immediately after the cross-country season. Our poor showing in the National the week before gave us little hope of a win but we were soon to be proved wrong. Dave Baulch took the first stage and brought us in a creditable fourth in 18m.3s., twenty-three seconds behind the leaders, Thames Valley. Eric Gebbett ran the second stage in 18.45 and took us up to third with T.V.H. still in first place, forty-three seconds ahead. Ranjit Bhatia did 18.28 on the third stage but was forced to give way to George Knight, who put up a lap record of 17.21, and we were back to fourth again. Polytechnic had gone into first place and forty-six seconds covered the first four teams. John Davies performed well to do 18.40 on the fourth lap and maintained his position although losing some ground to the leaders who were then over a minute ahead. Brian Hallowell was given the fifth stage and in doing 18.38 took us back to third, one minute and twelve seconds behind Poly who were still leading by one minute from Woodford Green Len Bishop kept us in third position with 19.02 but could not close the gap on Poly and Malcolm Robinson went off, 1.26 behind, on the seventh stage. His time of 18.53 was a little disappointing but it kept us in the same position. Woodford had taken over the lead from Poly and we were lagging by over 1½ min. Charlie Walker, on the eighth stage, was also disappointing with 18.49 and dropped us back to fourth after a battle royal over the last half-mile with Alan Perkins(Ilford) and Bert Ingles (T.V.H.). Pat Newell was in good form and, with an excellent time of 18.09, brought us up to second, exactly one minute behind Woodford, and it was left to John Moore, on the last stage, to hold this position with Woodford the winners in a course record time and T.V.H. third. 1st Woodford Green A.C. 3h.4m.42s; 2nd Belgrave 3h.6m.25s. 3rd Thames Valley H. 3h.7m.14s. items.s: R.W.A. 10 MILE CHAMPIONSHIP. MARCH 21ST. Report of the R.W.A. 10 mile walking championship at Sheffield, where Belgrave won the team title with Stan Vickers second, plus a list of members walking for their counties. To arrive at ST. Pancras station and find our Hon. Secretary rubbing shoulders with Tommy Trinder made me think that Jack Goswell's musical talents had been rejected and that our Hon. Treasurer had spared no expense to ensure the happiness and comfort of our team. However, it turned out that Fulham F.C's. supporters were travelling on the same train and they obviously felt that Alf had talents which could be of use to them. Altogether seventeen of us travelled to Sheffield where coaches were waiting to take us to the venue. The course was a typical Northern one of the out and back variety with some pretty stiff climbs on the way out. From the start "Claret and Gold" dominated the proceedings with Stan Vickers challenging Matthews, the eventual winner. Stan was not, unfortunately, at his best, having only recently recovered from 'flu and Matthews went right away, to win by over two minutes. Eric Hall gave one of his usually polished performances to finish third, and he was followed by George Williams who walked in excellent style. A ding-dong battle for 4th team position developed between the two Rays(Hall and Middleton), which Ray Hall eventually won by proving the stronger over the last two miles. Terry Clark gave a creditable display in his first Senior R.W.A. championship. It is unfortunate that the times are suspect owing to a misunderstanding at the turning point. The journey home was enlivened by the usual musical interlude from J.W.G., which does so much to soothe and quieten a tired body and mind. items.s: T.V.H. ROAD RELAY AT CRANFORD - MARCH 28TH Stage-by-stage report of the T.V.H. road relay at Cranford, used as Brighton relay preparation, with Belgrave 'A' finishing eighth. We entered five teams for this event which we were supporting for the first time for many years. The main object was to give our runners experience of this type of competition as a preparation for the Brighton relay and also to make last minute selections for this race. A number of those entered could not attend and we eventually started four teams of which three finished. The runners on the first stage were Walker(A), Collis(D), L. Bishop(C), and E. Bishop(E). Collis led our boys home in seventh place with a time of 23.49 against the leaders (St. Albans) 22.52. Walker was 12th with 24.24, Len Bishop 17th in 24.57 and Eric Bishop 26.02. Jim Heathfield took over from Collis on the second stage for the 'D' team with Bhatia running for the 'A', Shippen for the 'C' and Conway for the 'E'. Ranjit, with a time of 24.15, caught and passed Jim to finish 10th., Jim being in 11th place, Clive 13th and Conway 26th. Archie Bedford continued for the 'A' and did 24.30 to retain 10th position. Eddie Short, running for the 'C' remained in 13th place but Dennis Jones dropped the 'D' back to 14th. The 'E' team had shot its bolt and had no runners on this stage. The fourth and last stages were run by M. Robinson(A) who did 24.14 to take us up to 8th, J. Masters(C) who did 24.43 moved up to 12th and David Jones(D) who fell back to 15th. Colin Collis really pulled one out of the bag to be our only runner under 24min. and earned his place in the Brighton team. It was grand to see Colin running so well. The remainder of the times were very mediocre compared with performances by other clubs. items.sum: Syd Roberts's account of an R.W.A. Southern Committee dinner at which Stan Vickers received record plaques, the International Trophy and the Fowler Dixon Style award.
items.s: R.W.A. HONOURS STAN VICKERS Syd Roberts's account of an R.W.A. Southern Committee dinner at which Stan Vickers received record plaques, the International Trophy and the Fowler Dixon Style award. On 12th March a dinner was held at the "Feathers" Hotel, St. James's, S.W.1., sponsored by the R.W.A. Southern Committee, the main purpose of which, was to present British Native and British All Comers' Record Plaques to Stan Vickers for his new records which he set up last year. Whilst the function was not too well supported, Belgravians constituted about half the total assembly. Norman Easlea, Vice President of the A.A.A. and a past President of the R.W.A., in presenting the two plaques to Stan, gave a glowing account of his achievements over the past three years culminating in his outstanding performance at Parliament Hill last September. Norman was followed by Timber Woodcock who then presented to Stan the new International Trophy for the most outstanding performance in International Competition during 1958. This trophy, a very handsome one, was won by the British Team in Italy in 1957 and has a Belgrave interest as George Checkley was a member of that team. Permission was subsequently given by the British Board for it to be adopted as an International Trophy. Further tributes were then paid to Stan by Alf McSweeney whose club promoted the race in which Stan set the new records, by Ernest Neville who also presented to Stan the Fowler Dixon Style award which he won in the A.A.A. Championships last year, and Harold Whitlock who spoke of the great assistance given by Stan to other members of the team in the European Championships at Stockholm. Having been well and truly loaded up with trophies Stan was then called upon to reply and he made it quite clear that without the assistance of numerous people he is quite certain that he would never have broken any records. He mentioned, in particular, Ray Hall who endured all sorts of agonies in accompanying Stan during training and Matthews of Sutton Coldfield who battled with him during the actual race. A further presentation to one of the retiring R.W.A. Auditors and the customary toast of the Chairman completed a most enjoyable and interesting evening. items.sum: Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County.
items.s: NATIONAL LONDON-BRIGHTON RELAY - APRIL 11TH. Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County. The report on this race can usually be made interesting but how can anyone raise enthusiasm over a team which at no time during the whole race was higher than tenth and at one stage was as far back as sixteenth? The tale of woe really began during the week prior to the race when firstly John Davies was forced to withdraw because of foot trouble and then Clive Shippen contracted enteritis and had to stand down. John had been allocated the first leg and this was given to Charlie Walker who could not, this year, impress the selectors sufficiently to gain more than the first reserve designation. A quick switch of Eric Gebbett from the fifth to the fourth leg let in Jim Masters on the Redhill stage which has almost become his own property by divine right. The race started in fine weather but soon after Purley was passed ( we joined the race at this well known place as our Cross-Country Secretary resides there!) it began to rain. Our spirits were at a very low ebb on finding our team back in 13th place, and the weather did nothing to improve them. They were raised subsequently, for brief intervals, at the prospect of a position in the first half of the field! The whole story is most dismal; Charlie Walker struggled into tenth place on the first leg in a poor time, Malcolm Robinson floundered along on the second and lost three places, his time of 26.18 being the fifteenth best of the day, and Colin Collis,who was entrusted with the vital stage from Mitcham to Purley after his brilliant run in the T.V.H. relay, had an almost complete breakdown and finished in a distressed condition in 15th place. At this point we were 3m.42s. behind Coventry Godiva who were then leading. We now hoped that Eric Gebbett would redeem our fate but this was not to be and we remained in the same position but dropped to 4m.24s. behind the leaders, Derby and County, who were never again to be headed. Even Jumbo Masters could do nothing to put the matter right and fell back to 16th with a gap of 5m.55s. between us and Derby. Truly a hopeless position but Alan Black set out to prove that his loss of form over the previous few weeks was purely temporary and with the fifth fastest time of the day brought us back to 14th. Archie Bedford, although on the wrong side of forty, put up a plucky effort across Gatwick Aerodrome and, despite being forced to give way to Shaftesbury, can be said to have run true to form. Pat Newell must have been very dispirited waiting for well over six minutes after the leaders had passed by for his turn to come and this obviously affected his performance, for he could make no impression on those ahead and remained in fourteenth place. Next came Dave Baulch, making his last appearance for Belgrave (so he says), and he set off as though he really meant Belgrave to reach Brighton first. Running with more zest than most of the team put together he whipped past two of the opposition and took us to twelfth. Bhatia, on his first, and we sincerely hope not his last Brighton, took over in cold, wet and dreary conditions far from suitable for his type of running and, with a very good effort, he gained one more place. John Moore could make no more progress and Brian Hallowell on the last stage was over two minutes behind the team in front and could do no more than maintain his position despite a time which was the fourth fastest of the day. Inquests gain nothing but it is evident we must look for new faces before the October race for Southern Clubs. On this showing I would forecast that only Alan Black, Dave Baulch, Renjit Bhatia and Brian Hallowell will retain their places in the team - I wonder how right I shall be. items.sum: Report of the club 20 miles walk championship, led from the start by Eric Hall, with Cyril Yescombe third in a big personal best.
items.s: CLUB 20 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP - APRIL 18TH Report of the club 20 miles walk championship, led from the start by Eric Hall, with Cyril Yescombe third in a big personal best. Perverse Mother Nature was in a cold and boisterous mood when our walkers faced the starter for the 20 miles Championship. Once again we welcomed some visitors from the Met. Police A.C. in the field of eighteen starters. Eric Hall went into the lead immediately, accompanied by Terry Clark who only completed two laps of the course. Halfway times were not outstanding; Eric and Terry Clark were still leading with Ray Hall in 3rd place closely followed by Cyril Yescombe and George Beecham who were about three minutes in front of George Checkley. Johnny Morris was walking a very steady race but one or two of the back men were travelling too fast and suffered from the cold in the later stages of the race. Over the last five miles George Beecham dropped back to fifth place after an unhappy time but Cyril Yescombe held on to third place and, having walked his fastest 10 miles in the first part of the race, completed the course in a very fast time which was over 10 minutes better than he had ever done before. This split the handicap wide open and Cyril treated us to an even bigger and better grin. Johnny Morris's steady walking (20 miles at an almost identical speed each mile) gave him second handicap prize. Eric improved on the previous best time for the race on this course by over twenty seconds and gained third handicap prize. And so to Imber Court with a true Belgravian effort for the 'National 20'. items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham.
items.s: FROM THE HON. SECRETARY Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham. It is with considerable pleasure that we advise the appointment of Les Stokell as Junior Hon. Secretary.His address is:- 174, Frant Road, Thornton Heath, Surrey, and all our junior members are asked to record this address on their summer fixture card, and make themselves known to Les at the earliest opportunity. He will, of course, work in close cooperation with other Club officers; and we expect, under Les Stokell's guidance, to see the younger element in the Club progressively go from success to success. Les is probably the ideal man for the job he has undertaken. As a schoolmaster he will know the problems of the younger member, as a qualified Physical Training Instructor he is in a position to advise and assist on many athletic problems. As a former member of our teams and as an International runner (he represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games) Les has a lot of knowledge to impart and experience to pass on; as a strong personality with tremendous enthusiasm and competence he can well become one of the greatest assets Belgrave have ever had. We were pleased to have greetings and good wishes recently from Mr. F.A. Bool, a Life Member, who became Hon. Secretary of the Club in 1899, and succeeded A.H.N. Edwards who had occupied this position for the first twelve years of the Club's existence. Mr Bool recalls the early racing, including sprints, on the Embankment. Still resident in Chelsea he follows the Club's activities with the greatest interest. Len Fletcher, one of our great walkers from 1925 onwards, is again in West Middlesex Hospital; but it is now hoped that a new course of treatment will bring almost complete recovery. We sincerely hope so and send Len all good wishes. Congratulations and thanks to Frank Simmons on the success of the winter coaching and training sessions at Chelsea Barracks. No doubt the hard work done there will be reflected in better performances than ever before on the track this coming season. Very special attention is called to our Track Championships on Saturday June 6th at HURLINGHAM PARK TRACK, S.W.6 and it is hoped that every Club member will come along and bring his friends. There is ample accommodation for all. It is hoped also that our athletes will show their appreciation of an excellent track and first class arrangements and give us bumper entries in all events, and keenly fought out Championships. Hurlingham Track is easily reached from Putney Bridge Station (District Line), and many bus routes run nearby. There is ample car parking accommodation at the track. Let's make this a really memorable occasion! Les Stokell Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary; schoolmaster and PT instructor; represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games F.A. items.sum: The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY SECRETARY'S NOTES The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit. These notes will reach you well after the end of the cross-country season but I hope you will forgive me for recapping on the winter activities. To say that the overall results were disappointing is putting it mildly. At the beginning of September I was hopeful that 1958/9 would start a revival for Belgrave and we would recover some of our lost glory but the Surrey Road Relay at Woking found us taking a back seat behind Herne Hill, Walton and South London. The following week we took part in the Polytechnic Relay (8 x 3 miles) and it was encouraging to finish three complete teams. The 'A' team were fifth, the 'B' team were ninth for which they qualified for the medals awarded to the first 'B' team, and the 'C' team twenty-fifth. Good times were recorded by Baulch, Bhatia, Davies and Newell. These two races,followed by our own 5¾ miles road race and 3 miles yacht handicap, preceded the London to Brighton Relay for Southern clubs on October 11th and we had every reason to think we were set for a place - in actual fact we had to struggle hard to secure sixth place to qualify for the National Relay in April. On October 25th we revisited Chelmsford for their annual relay after an absence of some years. A strong team,on paper,took eighth place, 2½ minutes behind Woodford. A cross-country relay at Reigate Priory on November 1st gave us seventh place with minor clubs like Deptford Park, Brighton, Hercules and Rochester ahead of us. On November 22nd we lost our hold on the L.C.C. Championship, taking third place behind Highgate and Queens Park Harriers. Charlie Walker and John Moore did well to take 8th and 10th places respectively. The first major cross-country race, the South of the Thames Junior, was held at Epsom Downs on November 8th and Ken Miller(20th), John Moore(26th), Malcolm Robinson(34th) and Clive Shippen(35th) ran well to give us 3rd team award behind South London and Walton. For the next two months we engaged in inter-club fixtures with reasonable success and also held our 7 miles Championship in which Charlie Walker caught Pat Newell on the wrong foot and, against the form book, chalked up another win in this race. The first Saturday in January is always set aside for the county championships and this year the Surrey race was held at Epsom Downs. Although we packed well together we could do no better than fifth, with South London, Herne Hill, Walton and Surrey A.C. taking the earlier positions. Malcolm Robinson was unfortunately forced to retire when well placed, thus depriving us of a possible place. The 10 miles Championship on January 24th reversed the result of the "seven" and gave Pat Newell an easy win over Walker with John Moore again taking third place. Eight minutes covered the first twelve runners, a very wide spread and not very encouraging for the big championships to follow in February and March. The first of these was the South of the Thames Senior which was held from our own headquarters at short notice owing to extensive flooding at the planned venue at Maidenhead. This is a race which we have won on a number of occasions and most of our leading runners are ineligible. Nevertheless our twelfth position was far from satisfactory over our own familiar terrain. The winning team Portsmouth, finished seven men before our first runner, John Moore, who was 49th, and South London, who were second, placed six men in front of John! On February 14th we travelled to Aylesford for the Southern and were surprised by the much improved running of our team which took fifth place with 345 points after T.V.H.(169), Woodford(208), Portsmouth(283) and S.L.H.(305). It was grand to see the lads making steady progress throughout the race - another five miles would probably have secured us a place! Special mention should be made of Pat Newell who took 14th position in very good company - a great effort. Three weeks later the National was held from the Hotpoint Factory at Peterborough but the hope of a good position, after our improved form in the Southern, did not materialize and we scored a record number of points - 980. Let the individual positions speak for themselves - Newell 59th, Shippen 136th, Baulch 158th, Gebbett 174th, Bedford 205th and Walker 248th. The annual visit to Ilford for the local club's relay followed the National by seven days and produced second place behind Woodford Green who beat the course record with 3h.4m.42s. Our time of 3h.6m.25s. is the second best we have shown over this course. Strangely enough it was five years ago when we caned the record to win in 3h.6m.1s. - is this a reflection on our present strength when times generally are much faster? On March 21st we held our road Championship and Pat Newell added yet another victory to his ever growing list of Club Championships with a record breaking run of 28m.21s. Dave Baulch took second place and Malcolm Robinson was third. We visited Cranford for the T.V.H. road relay on Easter Saturday and started four teams but were without a number of our best performers, and in consequence were not in the running for leading honours. The 'A' team were 8th, the 'C' team 12th and the 'D' team 15th. Colin Collis, in a welcome return to form, produced the fastest time of our boys. The last effort of the winter season is the National Relay over the London to Brighton course. Our team on paper appeared to be our best for some years, but again we were to be greatly disappointed and, after much floundering in the lower half of the field, we could do no better than 11th for the second year in succession, some nine minutes behind the winners, Derby and County A.C. Now we have to qualify in the race for Southern clubs in October in order that the "Claret and Gold" shall be seen on the Brighton road next April. Thus the season came to an end on a despondant note and my hopes of six months earlier had not been realised, A few bright specks in the shape of the Southern and the Ilford relay, in an otherwise dark sky indicate that our prospects may not be as poor as they would appear. In fact I know that our past glories will return, but not before we have all taken complete stock of ourselves. Athletes and Officials alike must change their ideas. Obviously a club having a membership such as ours must again come to the fore, but if this is to be accomplished we must discard obsolete methods of training which produce a general fitness but do not bring the speed and strength required for the modern level of athletics. Circuit training and regular exercises with the weights must become standard to the schedules of everyone, not just the few. This combined with longer and more varied running sessions, a la Herb Elliott, will ensure faster times and increased confidence. It only needs an average improvement of 45 seconds per man for us to again win a Brighton relay and to reduce our National score by over 500 points. This improvement is well within the capabilities of many of our runners and with the advent of our leading juniors such as Alan Black, Ken Miller, Chris Thompson, Alan Peckings and Derek Crookes, to mention just a few, in to senior competition with, I hope, the return of such performers as George Flanagan, Charlie Dabbs and Ron Linstead, I look to the future with considerable anticipation. If small clubs like Derby, Sheffield and Portsmouth and clubs like South London and Thames Valley who are no larger than ourselves can do well then so can we. Therefore I want you all to analyse your training methods to see where you went wrong - set yourself an improved target and don't give up until it is attained. Use Club events throughout the year to achieve your ambition and don't be sidetracked by other subsidiary interests. Remember that in trying to put Belgrave back on the map you yourself may also attain honours and I can assure you that there is nothing more satisfying than winning your county colours as a prelude to representative and International recognition. A revival of that pre-war spirit which took a small group of our members to team and individual honours, in combination with a greater attention to training, will produce the results which, I am sure, are not far away. Why not start now to build up that spirit by getting together with other members and resolving to become Belgravians whose names will be added to that select roll of "never to be forgottens". A sense of friendly rivalry will do much to gain this object - go to it!! Baulch Baulch 158th National Bhatia Bhatia Davies Davies Newell Newell 59th National Charlie Walker Charlie Walker 8th L.C.C. items.s: CROSS-COUNTRY SEASON 1958-9 Tribute to Arthur Whitehead's organisation of eleven cross-country events using Club facilities in 1958-9, with the list of events and duties. It is impossible to estimate the benefits that "back room" workers bring to hundreds of participants in the great winter activity of cross-country running. We are indebted to Arthur Whitehead for his organisation and assistance in the following events which, during the past year, have involved the use of Club facilities. Needless to say no other club approaches the help and co-operation we give to the sport and none can boast of such a competent band of workers as that which Arthur has at his disposal. This is not only a substantial contribution to the sport but a great encouragement to competitors. In addition it is felt that the Club must benefit by the wide publicity obtained through acknowledgements in the programmes of the events concerned and also by the fact that our colours are in evidence at all these meetings. items.sum: Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials.
items.s: TRACK SECRETARY'S NOTES Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials. Members should by now have received their fixture cards for the track season and it is hoped that all concerned will note that they are expected to support all Club fixtures - it is, in fact, an obligation. I would like to point out that these fixtures do not arrange themselves, but that a vast amount of work is put in by Section Secretarys, Captains and Vice Captains to make a coherent programme. If you have any queries, get in touch with your section Secretary, Captain or Vice Captain. Don't wait for them to come to you - go to them. Tell them what you are doing in training or what you mean to do. They can only help you if you help yourself. All the best! Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd

items.sum: Report of Belgrave's senior and junior performances in a track match against Mitcham, Deptford Park and Surrey A.C. at Carshalton.
items.s: MATCH v. MITCHAM, DEPTFORD PARK & SURREY A.C. - CARSHALTON,MAY2ND. Report of Belgrave's senior and junior performances in a track match against Mitcham, Deptford Park and Surrey A.C. at Carshalton. Despite a rather weak representation, those of our men who did turn up performed quite creditably. Seniors Charlie Jones took second place in both sprints, clocking 10.2 and 22.9; in the second string Alan Jackson was third in 23.9. In the 440 Dave Mitchell was second in 53.4 whilst Alan Jackson won the second string event in 53.5. A very good performance came from John Thresher who finished third in the 'half' in 1m.59.7s.In the second string event Dave Taylor was second in 2m.9s. Malcolm Robinson, improving every time out, recorded 4m.26s. to take third place in the mile, his fastest time to date, whilst Alan Black was fourth in the second string event in 4m.37.6s. As this meeting clashed with the Sward Trophy we were poorly represented. In the Senior events, John McNaughton and Bob Taylor reached the 100 yds. final, which John won in 10 4 with Bob 4th suffering from a pulled muscle. Alan Peckings was our only representative in the mile but found the pace too fast ; the winner was M. Barratt of Ealing in 4m.19s. John Thresher again beat 2 minutes in the 880 yds. taking 3rd place behind Blagrove. In the same event Dave Taylor did 2m.6s. Don MacLean was our fastest man in the 2 miles, finishing 3rd in 9m.56s..Our other runners were K. Miller (10m4s.) David Jones(10m.22s.) and Ted Pallent(10m.50s.) items.sum: The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters.
items.s: EDITORIAL The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters. Dear Fellow Members, In all probability this is the last Belgravian editorial which will flow from this pen, for it is hoped that new editors will take over the magazine after September. We feel that our contribution over the last few years, though small, has helped to ensure the recording of Club activities, successes and failures, and, we trust, in a manner and vein acceptable to most. We have not pleased everyone all of the time and have not been immune from personal attack (once for something we didn't even write!). But the magazine is there for everyone to air his views and the greater the interest of any individual in Club affairs the more eager he becomes to expound his theories and invite criticism. And what better way than through the Belgravian? We are indebted to Clive Shippen for his well prepared reports, to Alf Harley, whose knowledge of Club history is second to none and whose writings are always of such great interest, and to all those members whose contributions have enabled us to produce the magazine during our term as editors. It is our hope that even greater support will be extended to the new editors. In passing we must pay tribute to the great efforts being made by Les Stokell and Tom Carter in recruiting and training the fine band of youngsters who are now so successfully performing in Belgrave colours. Here lies our chance to build future teams of National class and we ask that all members, old and young, see to it that the necessary words of encouragement are given to these lads; we all know what it means to be noticed "by those who matter". items.sum: The Hon. Secretary's notes: a timekeeping qualification for E.T. Ryan, a visit from Wally Bayliss, Jack Bidgood's M.B.E., an athletics clinic introduced by Don Brown, and tickets for the White City Floodlit Meeting.
items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes: a timekeeping qualification for E.T. Ryan, a visit from Wally Bayliss, Jack Bidgood's M.B.E., an athletics clinic introduced by Don Brown, and tickets for the White City Floodlit Meeting. We congratulate our Vice-President E.T. Ryan on qualifying to be added to the list of First-grade Timekeepers. He is a very worthy addition and we count ourselves fortunate on having his services and of our ever-reliable Dick Savage. How nice to see our former President, and Hon. Secretary for 11 years, Wally Bayliss, at one of our evening meetings recently. Welly was a great figure in our Club life for many years and his wager (hush!) of a pound to a penny on Belgrave when they held a commanding lead in the Brighton Relay, which was lost in the last few yards, has become one of the Club legends. Let's see you again soon, Wally! Congratulations to Vice-President Jack Bidgood on the award of the M.B.E. in the Queen's Birthday Honours List. We know it to be well deserved. We have had the very good fortune to be introduced to a private Athletics Clinic in the Knightsbridge area, equipped with the most modern apparatus and staffed by qualified physiotherapists with a very deep interest in our sport. Already one of our Olympic athletes has had successful curative treatment of an injury and other prominent members have received the benefit of the most modern treatments at nominal cost. We are indebted to our former Champion and member of many years standing, Don Brown, for this valuable introduction; and any members who feel they would benefit from the facilities available should, in the first instance, contact Don at Kensington 3336 for an appointment to be made. Our Club benefits financially each year from the promotion of the Floodlit Meeting (this year on Sept. 30th) at the White City. You will help yourself athletically by witnessing one of the finest meetings of the season - as this promotion always is; and you will be assisting our Club and many others that we meet in sporting rivalry if you go along. Tickets at all prices may be booked through Frank Webb, 50 Longford Avenue, Southall, Middx., but it must be done quickly. E.T. Ryan E.T. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H.
items.s: SWARD TROPHY MEETING Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H. May 9th brought round "The Sward" once again at Chiswick. On paper our team was, I think, the strongest we have ever been able to enter, but injuries, illness and other matters seriously depleted it. As we have no really adequate reserves we were unable to supply competitors in the 120 yds. hurdles, Pole Vault, Discus or High Jump. Tolson had pulled a muscle, Norman Caves had contracted tonsilitis, Andorka was sitting very important exams and Mal Ash threatened to retire; I was unable to change his mind. However, those who did turn out put up some fine performances and I am sure that, with the help of our absentees, we could have troubled L.A.C. and T.V.H. who tied for the trophy. Percy Porter gave us a good start with 4th place in the hammer (155'9"), Derek McCorquindale, in his first outing for Belgrave, showed his class and won the shot with 49'0¼" and our Captain Dave Ansell took second place in the long jump with 21'4½" and, deputising for Norman Caves, 5th in the triple jump at 42'3½" (a personal best). Charlie Jones had his first outing over the 440 yds. hurdles and was 5th in 58·8s. He is bound to improve a lot on this with more competition and increased confidence. John Sams, who last year won the A.A.A. Junior 200 yds. hurdles, was running for the first time as a senior in the 220 yds. hurdles. I am sure he was disappointed at not reaching the final but National Service and shortage of training took their toll. Next year perhaps a win! We also had Alan Black running only his second steeplechase as a senior. Unfortunately he bruised a heel on the third lap when landing from a hurdle and was forced to change his hurdling leg but with true Belgrave spirit he kept going and finished a very creditable 6th in 9m.53·7s. John Ware was our javelin man and he threw up to his early season form but 158'4" was not good enough for a place in that class of competition. We scored 19 points for 5th place out of eleven clubs. As usual there were some relays and running events for which we had invitations. Our 4 x 110 yds. team failed to materialize and in the 4 x 440 yds. we were fifth. Frank Wright, Pat Fox, Alan Jackson and Brian Morris constituted our team. The medley relay saw us finish in 6th place. We had only three men in the two miles team race and finished well down but Malcolm Robinson ran a personal best of 9m.24s. to finish seventh. C.J.
